SAL1 · Security Analyst L1.title: SAL1

cur.label: Current exam
cur.note: One exam, three parts, in order: 80 multiple-choice questions in 1 hour (200 points), then two SOC Simulator scenarios of 2 hours each (400 points each). All of it has to be done inside a 24-hour window that starts when you begin.
cur.onote: TryHackMe lists these five areas without weights. The bars are a suggested study share, tilted toward areas 3 to 5 because the SOC Simulator (80% of the score) leans on them.

domains.name: Fundamental Knowledge
obj: Network essentials
TCP/IP, common ports, DNS, HTTP and how normal traffic looks, so the strange traffic stands out.
Operating system basics
Windows and Linux processes, services, users, file systems and where each one keeps its logs.
Cryptography basics
Hashing versus encryption, certificates and TLS, and why encoded (Base64) is not encrypted.
Cloud and virtualisation basics
Virtual machines, containers and cloud accounts, and how they show up in your alerts.
Web and scripting basics
HTTP requests and responses, HTML and JavaScript, and reading PowerShell, Bash and Python well enough to tell what a script does.

domains.name: Cybersecurity Frameworks
obj: Cybersecurity fundamentals
The CIA triad, defense in depth, least privilege and the blue team's role.
MITRE ATT&CK
Tactics (the why), techniques and sub-techniques (the how), and mapping an alert to them.
Cyber Kill Chain
Recon, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions on objectives.
NIST Cybersecurity Framework
Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, and where a SOC sits in it.
Attack traces and indicators
IOCs (hashes, IPs, domains) versus behaviors, and the Pyramid of Pain.

domains.name: Common Malicious Behaviour
obj: Social engineering
Phishing, spoofed senders, lookalike domains and credential-harvesting pages. Read headers: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, Reply-To.
Network attacks
Port scans, brute force and password spraying, man-in-the-middle and data exfiltration.
Web exploitation
SQL injection, XSS, path traversal, file upload abuse and web shells, as they look in web server logs.
Endpoint attacks
Malicious macros, credential dumping, persistence through scheduled tasks, services and Run keys.
Command and control
Beaconing, DNS tunneling and traffic to new or rare domains.
Malware and LOLBAS
Malware types, and attackers living off the land with built-in tools like PowerShell, certutil and rundll32.

domains.name: Security Tools of the Trade
obj: Endpoint detection and response (EDR)
Process trees, isolating a host, and reading what ran, from where and by whom.
Network and web protection
Firewalls, IDS/IPS (Snort rules), proxies and web application firewalls.
Security information and event management (SIEM)
Searching logs in Splunk (SPL) and Elastic (KQL), building timelines and pivoting between fields.
Security orchestration and automation (SOAR)
Playbooks that enrich and respond automatically, and what still needs a human.
Threat intelligence platforms
Checking hashes, IPs and domains against threat intel (VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB and similar).
Vulnerability scanning
What scanners find, and why a scanner can set off alerts of its own.

domains.name: SOC Workflows and Activities
obj: SOC team and responsibilities
L1, L2 and L3 roles, and what Tier 1 owns: the alert queue.
Common security activities
Monitoring, triage, phishing review, threat hunting support and reporting.
Alert triage and ticketing
Classify true or false positive, set severity, document evidence and close or hand off.
SOC metrics and lookups
MTTD, MTTA, MTTR, false positive rate, and lookup tables and workbooks that speed up triage.
Escalation and communication
When and how to escalate, what to put in the ticket, and writing a clear case report.

pbqs.title: Triage the alert queue
pbqs.scenario: You're the L1 analyst on shift. For each alert, pick the verdict and the right next step. Steps can repeat.

rows.req: WINWORD.EXE on HR-PC07 started powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc ..., which then connected to a domain registered yesterday.
rows.why: Word starting hidden, encoded PowerShell that calls a brand-new domain is a classic malicious macro. It's real and needs response, so escalate with the evidence.

rows.req: Impossible travel: jlee logged in from Virginia, then from Frankfurt 5 minutes later. The Frankfurt IP is the company's own VPN exit, and jlee was on VPN.
rows.why: The 'travel' is the VPN. Document why it's benign and close it.

rows.req: Possible data exfiltration: 40 GB from BACKUP-01 to the backup vendor's known IP at 01:00. It has fired at 01:00 every night for six months.
rows.why: It's the approved backup, and it fires every night. Close it and ask for a tuning change that excludes this known flow, so the queue stops filling with it.

rows.req: certutil.exe on FIN-LT03 downloaded payload.exe to C:\Users\Public. Its hash is flagged by 12 antivirus engines.
rows.why: A built-in tool abused to download a known-bad file. Escalate so the host is contained and the payload is investigated.

rows.req: A user reported a phishing email with a credential page. Mail logs show nobody clicked, and the email gateway already pulled the message from every inbox.
rows.why: The phishing was real (true positive), but it's contained and nobody clicked. Record the IOCs and close it. Nothing is left for L2.

pbqs.title: Name what the log shows
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from your SIEM. Pick what it shows. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log:
38 x EventCode=4625  user=jsmith  src=185.220.101.4  (02:11:05 to 02:12:40)
1 x  EventCode=4624  user=jsmith  src=185.220.101.4  LogonType=10
items.why: Dozens of failures for one account from one outside IP, then a successful RDP logon (type 10). The guessing worked: escalate and reset the account.

items.log:
ParentImage: C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\WINWORD.EXE
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
CommandLine: powershell -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0A...
items.why: Word starting hidden PowerShell with an encoded command is the classic macro attack. Decode the Base64 to see what it does.

items.log:
10.0.0.1 - - "POST /uploads/img_442.php?cmd=whoami HTTP/1.1" 200 31
10.0.0.1 - - "POST /uploads/img_442.php?cmd=net+user HTTP/1.1" 200 812
items.why: A .php file in the uploads folder taking commands in a cmd parameter is a web shell. Someone uploaded code and is now running commands on the server.

items.log:
WS-18 TXT? aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ.x7k.example
WS-18 TXT? dGhpcyBpcyBkYXRh.x7k.example
WS-18 TXT? c2VjcmV0cyBoZXJl.x7k.example  (900 queries in 10 min)
items.why: Hundreds of TXT lookups with long, random-looking subdomains of one domain means data is being carried inside DNS queries.

items.log:
EventCode=4698  A scheduled task was created
Task Name: \Microsoft\Windows\Update\Updater
Action: C:\Users\Public\svc.exe   Trigger: At logon
items.why: A task disguised as an update that runs a file from C:\Users\Public at every logon. That's persistence.

items.log:
src=10.0.4.22 dst=198.51.100.7:443 bytes_out=2.1 GB time=02:13
(30-day average for 10.0.4.22: under 50 MB a day)
items.why: A huge outbound transfer at 2 AM from a host that normally sends almost nothing points to data leaving the network.

extras.title: Triage one alert
rows: Read the alert: rule name, host, user, time and severity.
Get context: who is the user, what is the host, is this normal for them?
Investigate in the SIEM and EDR: what happened before and after?
Check every IOC (hash, IP, domain) against threat intel.
Decide: true positive or false positive, with the evidence that proves it.
Escalate true positives that need action; close the rest with notes.
Write the case report: who, what, when, where, why and how.

extras.title: Windows events every L1 knows
rows: Logon type 2 is at the keyboard, 3 is over the network, 10 is RDP.
Many in a row from one source is brute force; one password across many users is spraying.
Needs command-line logging turned on to show the full command.
A new account outside a change ticket is a red flag.
A common way attackers survive a reboot.
Another persistence trick, and how PsExec shows up.
Almost never normal. Someone may be hiding tracks.
Parent and child process plus full command line and hashes.
Which process talked to which IP and port.

extras.title: Pyramid of Pain
extras.sub: 2.0 · how much it hurts the attacker
rows: Change one byte and the hash is new.
Registry keys, file paths, user agents.
They have to find or build new tools.
They have to change how they work. Detect these.

extras.title: SOC metrics
extras.sub: 5.0 · what your team is measured on
rows: Alert fires to an analyst picks it up.
Alert to the threat being contained.
Share of alerts that weren't real. High means rules need tuning.

keep.text: TryHackMe certs are valid for 3 years from the day you start the exam. Today you renew by passing the exam again.
keep.after: TryHackMe says renewal through a more advanced cert or related rooms is coming.

keep.text: SAL1 isn't on the DoD 8140 qualification matrix (V3.0). On its own it won't qualify you for a coded billet.
keep.after: Pair it with Security+ or CySA+, which are on the matrix, for analyst work roles like Cyber Defense Analyst (511).

keep.text: It proves you can triage a queue, which is exactly what Tier 1 interviews test. Add the badge to your résumé and LinkedIn with the verify link.
keep.after: In a Coast Guard SOC or a contractor interview, walk through one simulator case: alert, evidence, verdict, escalation.

The alert-queue tool the exam uses, with Splunk and an analyst VM. Start with the intro scenarios and repeat them until triage feels routine.
Real attack data to search in your own Splunk.
Investigation challenges on logs, PCAPs and phishing emails.
Look up every technique an alert maps to.
Windows tools attackers abuse, and how each one shows up.

tips: Close what you can prove
Close every alert you've worked before each 2-hour clock runs out. Alerts left open when time expires don't score.
Reports are points
Case reports are worth 100 of the 400 points in each scenario. Use who, what, when, where, why and how every time.
Don't over-escalate
Escalate true positives that need action. Escalating everything costs points like missing things does.
Pace the MCQ
80 questions in 60 minutes is 45 seconds each. Don't get stuck; it's only 200 of the 1,000 points.
Plan your 24 hours
It isn't proctored and you can break between parts, but the window runs nonstop once you start.

PT1 · Junior Pentester.title: PT1

cur.label: Current exam
cur.note: Three engagements, web application, network and Active Directory, each with its own scope and rules of engagement. You submit flags and write a report for each one. Candidates report a pass mark of 750 of 1000, with web worth the most.
cur.onote: TryHackMe lists these six areas without weights. The bars are a suggested study share, based on candidates reporting web at about 40% of the score, network about 36% and Active Directory about 24%.

domains.name: Reconnaissance and Enumeration
obj: WHOIS, DNS and subdomain discovery
Map the target's names and addresses before you touch anything else.
Nmap and port scanning strategies
Fast full-port sweeps first, then version and script scans on what's open.
Banner grabbing and service fingerprinting
Pin down exact software versions so you can look up known flaws.
Web and network account and service enumeration
Usernames, shares, directories, virtual hosts and API endpoints.
Exposed services and misconfigurations
Anonymous logins, default passwords, open shares and debug pages.

domains.name: Web Application Testing
obj: OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities
SQL injection, XSS, IDOR, SSRF and the rest, found and exploited by hand.
Manual testing techniques
Change one thing at a time and watch how the app responds.
Burp Suite
Proxy, Repeater, Intruder and Decoder: intercept, replay, fuzz and decode requests.
Authentication and session flaws
Weak logins, predictable tokens, missing logout and session fixation.
File upload and path traversal
Getting code onto the server, and reading files you shouldn't.
Bypassing client-side controls
Anything the browser enforces, the attacker can skip. Test the server.

domains.name: Network Penetration Testing
obj: SMB, RDP, FTP, SSH and SNMP
Find and exploit weak or misconfigured services on these ports.
Password attacks
Brute force and password spraying, and staying under the lockout limit.
Misconfigured and outdated services
Match versions to public exploits, and test default settings.
Pivoting and lateral movement
Use one compromised host to reach networks you couldn't before.
Sniffing, traffic analysis and man-in-the-middle
What you can capture on a network, and what it gives away.
Firewalls and network segmentation
Work out what's filtered, and find the paths that aren't.

domains.name: Active Directory Exploitation
obj: Kerberos attacks
AS-REP roasting and Kerberoasting, then cracking the hashes offline.
LDAP and domain enumeration
Users, groups, computers and policies, with or without credentials.
Misconfigured permissions and trusts
Rights like GenericAll or WriteDACL that hand you control of other objects.
Pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket
Log in with a stolen hash or Kerberos ticket instead of a password.
Privilege escalation in a Windows domain
From a normal user to domain admin, one step at a time.
BloodHound
Graph the domain and find the shortest path to the account you want.

domains.name: Exploitation and Post-Exploitation
obj: Metasploit and manual exploitation
Use frameworks when they fit, and know how to do it by hand when they don't.
Reverse and bind shells
Which one gets through the firewall, and how to make a shell stable.
File transfer
Moving tools and loot with HTTP servers, SMB shares, certutil, wget and scp.
Persistence and staging
How attackers keep access, and why you document anything you add.
Privilege escalation on Linux and Windows
Sudo rights, SUID files, weak services and stored credentials.
Operational security
Stay inside the rules of engagement and leave the lab as you found it.

domains.name: Reporting and Time Management
obj: Clear vulnerability reports
What it is, where it is, how you proved it and what it lets an attacker do.
Prioritizing findings by risk
Rank by impact and how easy it is to exploit, not by how fun it was.
Relevant mitigations
A specific fix for the root cause, not 'apply best practices'.
Managing a 48-hour window
Plan sleep, set time limits per target and move on when you're stuck.
Note-taking during a test
Commands, output and screenshots as you go, so the report writes itself.
Communicating attack paths and impact
Tell the story from first foothold to the flag, in order.

pbqs.title: Name the opening from the tool output
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from an authorized lab engagement. Pick the opening it shows. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log:
161/udp open  snmp  SNMPv1 server; community: public
| snmp-info:
|   enterprise: net-snmp
|_  engineIDFormat: unknown
items.why: SNMP answers with the default community public. Walk it with snmpwalk to pull users, processes and network details.

items.log:
Anonymous login successful

  Sharename       Type      Comment
  ---------       ----      -------
  IT_Backup       Disk      Nightly configs
  IPC$            IPC       Remote IPC
items.why: -N means no password, and it still listed shares. Connect to IT_Backup and look for configs with credentials in them.

items.src: Burp Repeater · logged in as bob
items.log:
GET /api/orders/5512 HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=bob...

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"order":5512,"owner":"alice","card_last4":"4417"}
items.why: Bob's session reads Alice's order just by changing the number. The server never checks who owns the order.

items.log:
[-] User jlee doesn't have UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH set
$krb5asrep$23$svc_print@CORP.LOCAL:7f3a9c...e21b
items.why: svc_print doesn't require pre-authentication, so you got its AS-REP without a password. Crack it with hashcat mode 18200.

items.log:
User www-data may run the following commands on web01:
    (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim
items.why: vim can run shell commands, and sudo runs it as root. sudo vim -c ':!/bin/sh' gives a root shell.

items.log:
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
www-data:x:33:33:www-data:/var/www:/usr/sbin/nologin
items.why: The page parameter is included from the file system, and ../ walks out of the web folder. Read config files next for credentials.

pbqs.title: Rate each finding and pick the fix
pbqs.scenario: You're writing the report. For each finding, pick a severity and the fix that addresses the root cause. Each fix is used once.

rows.req: Unauthenticated SQL injection on the internet-facing login page. It dumps every user's password hash.
rows.why: Anyone on the internet can exploit it with no account, and it exposes every credential. That's critical. Parameterized queries fix the root cause.

rows.req: Logged-in customers can read other customers' orders, including names and addresses, by changing the order number.
rows.why: It needs a login, but any customer can read everyone's data. That's high. The fix is checking ownership on the server for every request.

rows.req: SMB signing isn't required on internal file servers, so captured logins can be relayed by someone already inside the network.
rows.why: Serious, but the attacker must already be inside the network, so it's usually medium. Require signing on every host.

rows.req: The public web server's banner shows Apache/2.4.58.
rows.why: It only helps an attacker pick exploits. Low. Turn off version details in the server banner.

extras.title: Your 48 hours
extras.sub: All areas · one engagement at a time
rows: Read the scope and rules of engagement for the section. Note what's off-limits.
Recon: full port scan, then versions and scripts on open ports.
Enumerate every service: web paths, shares, users, versions.
Exploit the most promising path. Time-box each idea to about an hour.
Escalate privileges and grab the flags. Screenshot every step.
Write that section's findings while it's fresh, then move on.
Last block: proofread the report. It's graded, not just the flags.

extras.title: Ports to check first
rows: Anonymous login, readable or writable files
Reused or weak passwords, keys you've found
The web app: most of the points
A domain controller. AS-REP roast and Kerberoast
Null sessions, open shares, signing off
Community strings like public leak users and processes
Logins with sprayed or found credentials

extras.title: AD attacks at a glance
rows: Accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication turned off hand out a crackable hash (hashcat mode 18200).
Request tickets for accounts with an SPN and crack them offline (hashcat mode 13100).
One or two common passwords across every user, staying under the lockout limit.
Log in with the hash itself. No cracking needed.
Collect the domain's relationships and find the shortest path to Domain Admins.

extras.title: Anatomy of a finding
rows: What an attacker can do with it
Exact requests and commands, in order
A specific fix for the root cause

pbqs.title: Work the help desk queue
pbqs.scenario: Five tickets are waiting. For each one, pick the most likely cause and the best next step. Causes and steps can repeat.

rows.req: Laptop shows 169.254.10.4. Other users on the same switch are fine.
rows.why: APIPA means no DHCP offer arrived. Check the connection, then run ipconfig /release and /renew.

rows.req: PC can ping 8.8.8.8, but every browser says the server can't be found.
rows.why: Outside IPs answer, names don't. That's DNS: test with nslookup and check the DNS server setting.

rows.req: Static IP 10.5.5.20/24 with gateway 10.5.6.1. The user can print locally but can't reach anything off the subnet.
rows.why: 10.5.6.1 isn't in the 10.5.5.0/24 subnet, so the PC can't reach it. Set the gateway to the router's address in 10.5.5.0/24.

rows.req: Desk PC: no link light on the network card, and the switch shows the port as notconnect.
rows.why: No link on either end is physical. Reseat or swap the patch cable, then try another switch port.

rows.req: A user can open \\10.1.1.5\share by IP, but \\fileserver\share fails.
rows.why: By IP works, by name fails: the name isn't resolving. Check it with nslookup fileserver.

pbqs.title: Read the command output
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from a ticket. Pick what it shows. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log:
Interface   IP-Address  OK? Method Status                Protocol
Gi0/0       10.1.1.1    YES manual administratively down  down
items.why: “Administratively down” means someone ran shutdown on the interface. Enter the interface and run no shutdown.

items.log:
IPv4 Address. . . . : 169.254.88.3
Subnet Mask . . . . : 255.255.0.0
Default Gateway . . :
items.why: A 169.254 address with no gateway is APIPA: the PC never got a DHCP lease.

items.log:
> intranet.example.com
Server:  dns1.example.com
Address: 10.1.1.53
*** dns1.example.com can't find intranet.example.com: Non-existent domain
items.why: The DNS server answered, but has no record for that name. Check the spelling or add the record.

items.log:
1   <1 ms  <1 ms  <1 ms  10.1.1.1
2   10.1.1.1 reports: Destination net unreachable.
items.why: The gateway itself says it has no route to that network. The router needs a route (or a default route).

items.log:
GigabitEthernet1/0/5 is up, line protocol is up
  Half-duplex, 100Mb/s, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX
  4518 late collision, 2210 CRC
items.why: Half duplex with lots of late collisions and CRC errors is the classic duplex mismatch. Set both ends to auto, or both to the same fixed values.

items.log:
Vlan  Mac Address      Type     Ports
 30   0050.56aa.1b2c   DYNAMIC  Gi1/0/8
(Ticket: the printer on Gi1/0/8 belongs in VLAN 20, Printers)
items.why: The printer's MAC was learned in VLAN 30, so the port is assigned to the wrong VLAN. Move Gi1/0/8 to VLAN 20.

extras.title: Address ranges to know
rows: Self-assigned when DHCP fails. A clue, not a fix.

pbqs.title: Name the threat and pick the fix
pbqs.scenario: Four problems came in this week. For each one, name the threat and pick the control that would have stopped it. Each answer is used once.

rows.req: Hundreds of failed logins overnight against one account on the VPN portal, from many IPs.
rows.why: Password guessing at scale. MFA makes a guessed password useless, and lockout slows the guessing.

rows.req: An unknown Raspberry Pi is plugged into a conference room wall jack and has a network address.
rows.why: Network access control (802.1X) only lets known, authenticated devices onto a port.

rows.req: File shares are being renamed to .locked and a ransom note appears on the server.
rows.why: Ransomware. Offline backups it can't reach let you restore without paying.

rows.req: Users got an email “from the CO” asking them to sign in to a fake leave portal.
rows.why: Phishing. Filtering catches many messages, and training helps people report the rest.

pbqs.title: Read the endpoint and network evidence
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from a different tool. Pick what it shows. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log:
TCP  0.0.0.0:4444  0.0.0.0:0  LISTENING  6120
(PID 6120 = svch0st.exe in C:\Users\Public)
items.why: Port 4444 is a common backdoor port, and “svch0st” (with a zero) running from Public imitates a real Windows process.
Port 23 is Telnet, which sends everything in clear text, password included. Move to SSH.

items.log:
4625  An account failed to log on.  Account: admin  Source: 10.1.9.40
(57 events in 2 minutes)
items.why: Event 4625 is a failed logon. Dozens in minutes for one account is password guessing.
The gateway's IP points to the same MAC as another host, not the router's real MAC. The ARP cache has been poisoned.
One source trying a thousand ports in seconds is a port scan, mapping what's open.

items.log:
Threat: Trojan:Win32/Wacatac
File: C:\Users\jdoe\Downloads\invoice.exe
Action: Quarantine   Status: Succeeded
items.why: Defender found a trojan and quarantined it. Still check how it arrived and whether anything ran.

pbqs.title: Classify the alerts and act

rows.req: IDS alert “SQL injection” fired when a staff member searched the directory for the name O'Brien. The query was normal.
rows.why: The apostrophe in a real name tripped the signature. Nothing malicious happened, so tune the rule.

rows.req: An audit found a mailbox rule forwarding all of a user's mail outside for three weeks. No alert ever fired.
rows.why: A real compromise with no alert. Close the gap with a detection for new external forwarding rules.

rows.req: IDS flagged beacon traffic from FIN-07; EDR confirms an unknown process making the connections every 60 seconds.
rows.why: Two sources agree: it's real. Isolate the host and escalate with the evidence.

rows.req: No alerts overnight on the DMZ, and a log review shows only normal web traffic.
rows.why: No attack and no alert. Note the review and move on.

rows.req: Ops LAN: 100 hosts

rows.req: Admin LAN: 50 hosts
rows.why: 50 hosts need a /26 (62 usable). The next free block after .127 is 10.40.0.128, through .191.

pbqs.title: Diagnose from the output
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from a different trouble ticket. Pick what it shows. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log: %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH: Native VLAN mismatch discovered on GigabitEthernet0/1 (1), with SW2 GigabitEthernet0/1 (99).
items.why: CDP noticed the two ends of the trunk use different native VLANs. Set the same native VLAN on both.

items.log:
%SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port Gi1/0/14 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port.
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Gi1/0/14, putting Gi1/0/14 in err-disable state
items.why: A switch was plugged into a PortFast access port. Remove it, then shutdown and no shutdown the port.

items.log: %OSPF-4-ERRRCV: Received invalid packet: mismatched area ID from backbone area, from 10.1.1.2, GigabitEthernet0/0
items.why: The neighbor's hellos carry a different area ID, so no adjacency forms. Put both interfaces in the same area.

items.log:
R1# ping 172.20.5.1
.....
Success rate is 0 percent (0/5)
R1# show ip route 172.20.5.1
% Network not in table
items.why: The router has no route to that network and no default route. Add a static route or advertise it in OSPF.

items.log:
R1# show access-lists
Extended IP access list 110
    10 deny tcp any host 10.2.2.10 eq 443 (1882 matches)
    20 permit ip any any (90311 matches)
(Ticket: nobody can reach https on 10.2.2.10)
items.why: Line 10 is denying HTTPS to that server, and its match count keeps climbing. Fix or remove the line.

items.log:
Neighbor ID   Pri  State      Dead Time  Address    Interface
2.2.2.2         1  FULL/BDR   00:00:35   10.1.1.2   Gi0/0
items.why: FULL means the databases are synchronized. This neighbor is healthy, and the problem is elsewhere.

extras.title: How a router picks a route
rows: Longest prefix match wins: a /24 beats a /16 for an address in both.
Same prefix from different sources: lowest administrative distance wins.
Same source and prefix: lowest metric wins.
No match at all: use the default route (gateway of last resort), or drop the packet.

extras.title: Administrative distance
rows: The routing protocol on the CCNA.

rows.req: Unknown laptops plugged into conference room jacks get full network access.
rows.why: 802.1X (with MAB for printers and cameras) keeps ports closed until ISE says the device is allowed.

rows.req: Stolen passwords let attackers sign in to the cloud HR app from personal devices.
rows.why: Duo adds MFA and checks the device's trust before the app opens, so a password alone isn't enough.

rows.req: Contractors use a full-tunnel VPN, but should reach only one internal ticketing app.
rows.why: ZTNA (Secure Private Access) connects them to that one app instead of the whole network.

rows.req: Users working from home, off VPN, click links to newly registered malicious domains.
rows.why: DNS-layer security in Secure Access blocks bad domains wherever the user is.

rows.req: The data center's server VLAN needs IPS and URL filtering at its edge.
rows.why: An NGFW policy with intrusion prevention and URL filtering on Secure Firewall protects that edge.

pbqs.title: Read the security events
pbqs.scenario: Each event comes from a different Cisco or Splunk console. Pick what it shows. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log:
Event: Threat Quarantined
File: invoice_8812.exe   SHA-256: 9f2c...e1
Disposition: Malicious
items.why: Secure Endpoint judged the file malicious and quarantined it. Next, find out how it got there.

items.log: %DHCP_SNOOPING-5-DHCP_SNOOPING_UNTRUSTED_PORT: DHCP_SNOOPING drop message on untrusted port, message type: DHCPOFFER, MAC sa: 0011.2233.4455
items.why: A DHCP offer arrived on an untrusted port, so something other than the real server is handing out addresses. Snooping dropped it.

items.log: %SW_DAI-4-DHCP_SNOOPING_DENY: 1 Invalid ARPs (Res) on Gi1/0/7, vlan 20.([0011.2233.4455/10.20.0.1/...])
items.why: Dynamic ARP inspection dropped an ARP reply claiming the gateway's IP from a MAC that doesn't own it.

items.log:
AAA user authentication Rejected: reason = Invalid password: user = admin
(4,212 events from 198.51.100.77 in 10 minutes)
items.why: Thousands of failed logins against one account from one IP is password guessing. MFA and lockout policies stop it.

items.log:
host=WS-44  query=6a1f3b9c0e7d2a5f.qz-sync.example  type=TXT
(1,900 queries in 15 min, all unique subdomains)
items.why: Huge numbers of unique, encoded-looking subdomains of one domain carry data out inside DNS.

items.log:
CoA-Reauth sent to 10.0.0.12 port Gi1/0/9
Reason: endpoint profile changed to Axis-Camera
items.why: The profiler reclassified the device, so ISE sent a Change of Authorization to apply the right policy.

Study this one unless you already prepared for 1.6. At launch it's in English; LPI says French, German, Italian, Japanese, Portuguese and Spanish follow within a few months.
v20.onote: Official LPI objectives, version 2.0. Each objective's weight is about how many of the 40 questions it gets (shown at the start of each line). The bars show each topic's share.

obj: Linux Distributions
Weight 2. Kernel vs userspace, distro families (Debian, Enterprise Linux, SUSE, Alpine), release types like LTS, stable and rolling, and how Android relates to Linux.
Major Open Source Applications
Weight 2. Common desktop, web and server apps (Firefox, LibreOffice, Apache, NGINX, PostgreSQL, Samba), languages like Python and C, and package tools: apt, dnf, zypper, apk.
Open Source Software and Licensing
Weight 1. Free and open source ideas, copyleft (GPL) vs permissive (BSD) licenses, Creative Commons, the FSF and OSI.
Linux Usage
Weight 2. Where Linux runs (desktops, servers, VMs, cloud, embedded), the vi and nano editors, and safe habits: strong passwords, password managers, MFA, passkeys, HTTPS, careful USB use.

domains.name: Command Line Basics
obj: Command Line Usage
Weight 3. Bash syntax, variables, quoting, echo, history, PATH and export, and how a built-in differs from a program (type).
Documentation, Man Pages and Usage Information
Weight 2. man pages, -h and --help, and the docs in /usr/share/doc.
Files, Directories and Paths
Weight 2. ls and its options, cd, absolute vs relative paths, . and .., ~, hidden files, and finding files by name with find.
File and Directory Management
Weight 2. cp, mv, rm, touch, mkdir, rmdir, case sensitivity and simple wildcards (globbing).

domains.name: Data Processing
obj: File Archives and Compression
Weight 2. Create, list and extract tar and zip archives; gzip, bzip2 and xz.
Redirections and String Processing
Weight 3. Pipes, input and output redirection, and filtering text with grep (and grep -E), less, cat, head, tail, sort, uniq, cut and wc.
Shell Scripting Basics
Weight 4, the heaviest single objective. Scripts with #!/bin/bash, variables, arguments, if tests on files and variables, for loops over lists and wildcards, and exit status.

domains.name: Linux System Administration Basics
obj: Linux Installation and Provisioning
Weight 1. Installing on hardware, VMs and cloud instances; ISO files and images; dual boot; Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL).
Computer Hardware and Device Access
Weight 2. CPUs (x86, ARM), storage, NICs, drivers and kernel modules, device files in /dev, plus /boot, /sys, /dev/null, /dev/zero and /dev/urandom.
Processes and Log Messages
Weight 3. ps, top and free; start, stop and check services with systemctl; read logs with journalctl, dmesg and /var/log; /proc and /etc.
Network Configuration
Weight 2. IPv4 and IPv6 basics, routes, DNS, ip addr and ip route, ss, /etc/hosts and /etc/resolv.conf, resolvectl, DHCP and SLAAC, ping and host.

domains.name: Security and File System Permissions
obj: Remote Logins, File Transfers and Elevated Permissions
Weight 2. Root, standard and system users; sudo and su; ssh, scp, ssh-keygen and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
User and Group Management
Weight 2. /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group and /etc/skel; useradd, groupadd and passwd; who's logged in with id, w and last.
File System Permissions and Ownership
Weight 2. Read ls -l, change permissions with chmod and ownership with chown.
Special Directories and Files
Weight 1. /tmp and /var/tmp, the sticky bit, and symbolic links with ln -s.

Understanding Computer Hardware

Where Data is Stored

pbqs.title: Pick the command for each task
pbqs.scenario: You're on shift with a Linux terminal open. Pick the command that does each task. Each answer is used once; three are distractors.

items.text: Watch /var/log/auth.log and see new lines the moment they're written.
items.why: tail -f keeps the file open and prints new lines as they arrive.

items.text: Search /home for every file whose name ends in .sh.
items.why: find /home -name "*.sh" walks the directory tree and matches names. (locate was dropped from the 2.0 objectives and relies on a database that may be stale.)

items.text: Count how many lines are in users.txt.
items.why: wc -l counts lines.

items.text: Show only the lines in auth.log that contain “Failed password.”
items.why: grep prints the lines that match a pattern.

items.text: See which processes are using the most CPU right now, updating live.
items.why: top shows a live, sorted view of processes and resource use.

items.text: Check your user ID and every group you belong to.
items.why: id prints your UID, primary group and every group membership.

items.text: Read the full manual for chmod.
items.why: man chmod opens the manual page.

pbqs.title: Set the right permissions
pbqs.scenario: For each file or directory, pick the chmod number and the matching ls -l permission string.

rows.req: A private SSH key: only the owner can read and write it.
rows.why: 600 shows as rw------- in ls -l. SSH refuses to use a private key that other users can read.

rows.req: A team script: the owner has full control, the group can read and run it, others get nothing.
rows.why: 750 shows as rwxr-x---. 7 is rwx, 5 is r-x, 0 is nothing.

rows.req: A web page: everyone can read it, only the owner can change it.
rows.why: 644 shows as rw-r--r--, the normal setting for files.

rows.req: A case directory: the owner and the soc group can do everything in it, nobody else can enter.
rows.why: 770 shows as rwxrwx---. A directory needs x before anyone can enter it.

rows.req: An evidence file: the owner and group can read it, nobody can change it.
rows.why: 440 shows as r--r-----. Read-only for owner and group helps prevent accidental edits.

rows.req: A tool every user can run, but only the owner can change.
rows.why: 755 shows as rwxr-xr-x, the normal setting for programs.

pbqs.title: Read the Linux logs
pbqs.scenario: These lines came from journalctl and /var/log on a server you're watching. Pick what each one shows. Each answer is used once; two are distractors.

items.log:
sshd[2231]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.45 port 51122 ssh2
sshd[2231]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.45 port 51130 ssh2
sshd[2231]: message repeated 38 times
items.why: Many failed logins for a user that doesn't exist, from one outside address, is password guessing (brute force).

items.log: sshd[3310]: Accepted publickey for analyst from 10.4.2.15 port 50544 ssh2: ED25519 SHA256:q8V2...
items.why: “Accepted publickey” means the login used an SSH key, not a password.

items.log: sudo: jdoe : TTY=pts/1 ; PWD=/home/jdoe ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/cat /etc/shadow
items.why: jdoe ran a command as root through sudo, here reading the password hash file. Worth asking why.

items.log: useradd[4102]: new user: name=svc_backup, UID=1005, GID=1005, home=/home/svc_backup, shell=/bin/bash
items.why: useradd logged a new account. An unexpected new account with a login shell is a classic persistence sign.

items.log:
systemd[1]: nginx.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
systemd[1]: nginx.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.
items.why: systemd reports the service's main process exited with an error. Check systemctl status nginx and its config.

items.log:
usb 1-2: new high-speed USB device number 7 using xhci_hcd
usb-storage 1-2:1.0: USB Mass Storage device detected
items.why: The kernel detected a USB mass storage device. Many units restrict removable media, so this may need a report.

tips: Know the options
Questions often turn on one flag: -r, -f, -l, -i. Know what the common ones do.
Read the output
When a question shows ls -l or ps output, the answer is usually in one column.
Mind the order
2>&1 and > in the wrong order give a different result. Practice redirection until it's automatic.
Never leave a blank
There's no penalty for a wrong answer, so always pick something.

e101.label: Exam 101
e101.note: System architecture, installing Linux and managing packages, GNU and Unix commands, and devices, file systems and the directory layout. Commands are almost half of this exam. You can take 101 and 102 in either order.
e101.onote: Official LPI objectives, version 5.0. Each objective's weight is about how many of the 60 questions it gets. LPI removed 104.4, so the numbers skip it.

domains.name: System Architecture
obj: Determine and configure hardware settings
Weight 2. Enable devices, read hardware info from /sys, /proc and /dev, and use lsmod, modprobe, lspci and lsusb.
Boot the system
Weight 3. Firmware to boot loader to kernel to init; SysVinit vs systemd; read boot messages with dmesg and journalctl.
Change runlevels / boot targets and shutdown or reboot
Weight 3. Set the default target, switch targets (including rescue), shutdown, reboot and wall.

domains.name: Linux Installation and Package Management
obj: Design hard disk layout
Weight 2. Partitions for /, /var, /home and /boot, the EFI system partition, swap and basic LVM.
Install a boot manager
Weight 2. GRUB 2 basics: grub-install, grub-mkconfig, and editing boot options.
Manage shared libraries
Weight 1. ldd, ldconfig, /etc/ld.so.conf and LD_LIBRARY_PATH.
Use Debian package management
Weight 3. dpkg, apt-get and apt-cache: install, remove, find which package owns a file, list a package's files.
Use RPM and YUM package management
Weight 3. rpm, yum, dnf and zypper: install, query, verify signatures and map files to packages.
Linux as a virtualization guest
Weight 1. VMs vs containers, cloud instances, what to change on a cloned VM (SSH host keys, machine ID), cloud-init.

domains.name: GNU and Unix Commands
obj: Work on the command line
Weight 4. Variables, export, env, set, history, type and which, and running programs inside and outside PATH.
Process text streams using filters
Weight 2. cat, cut, sort, uniq, tr, head, tail, wc, sed, nl, split, zcat, and checksums with sha256sum.
Perform basic file management
Weight 4. cp, mv, rm, mkdir, find by type, size and time, tar, cpio, dd, gzip, bzip2 and xz.
Use streams, pipes and redirects
Weight 4. Redirect stdin, stdout and stderr; pipes; tee and xargs.
Create, monitor and kill processes
Weight 4. Jobs with &, bg, fg and nohup; ps, top, pgrep; signals with kill, pkill and killall; screen and tmux.
Modify process execution priorities
Weight 2. nice and renice; reading priority in ps and top.
Search text files using regular expressions
Weight 3. Basic vs extended regex; grep, grep -E and sed substitutions.
Basic file editing
Weight 3. vi modes, moving, editing, searching and saving (:w, :q!, ZZ); setting EDITOR.

domains.name: Devices, Linux Filesystems, Filesystem Hierarchy Standard
obj: Create partitions and filesystems
Weight 2. MBR and GPT with fdisk, gdisk and parted; mkfs for ext4, XFS, VFAT and exFAT; mkswap.
Maintain the integrity of filesystems
Weight 2. df and du for space and inodes; fsck, e2fsck, tune2fs and xfs_repair.
Control mounting and unmounting of filesystems
Weight 3. mount, umount, /etc/fstab, UUIDs and labels with blkid and lsblk; systemd mount units.
Manage file permissions and ownership
Weight 3. chmod, chown, chgrp and umask; SUID, SGID and the sticky bit.
Create and change hard and symbolic links
Weight 2. ln and ln -s; hard vs soft links; copy vs link.
Find system files and place files in the correct location
Weight 2. The FHS layout; find, locate and updatedb, whereis, which and type.

e102.label: Exam 102
e102.note: Shells and scripting, desktops and accessibility, admin tasks like users, cron and time zones, essential services (time, logging, mail, printing), networking and security.
e102.onote: Official LPI objectives, version 5.0. Each objective's weight is about how many of the 60 questions it gets.

domains.name: Shells and Shell Scripting
obj: Customize and use the shell environment
Weight 4. /etc/profile, ~/.bashrc and ~/.bash_profile, aliases, functions, export and source; /etc/skel.
Customize or write simple scripts
Weight 4. for, while, if and test, read, seq, command substitution, exit codes, && and ||, and the shebang.

domains.name: User Interfaces and Desktops
obj: Install and configure X11
Weight 2. X11 vs Wayland, xorg.conf, DISPLAY, xhost and xauth.
Graphical Desktops
Weight 1. KDE, GNOME and Xfce; remote desktops with VNC, RDP, Spice and XDMCP.
Accessibility
Weight 1. High contrast and large print, screen readers, magnifiers, on-screen keyboards, sticky and slow keys.

domains.name: Administrative Tasks
obj: Manage user and group accounts and related system files
Weight 5, the heaviest objective. useradd, usermod, userdel, groupadd, passwd, chage and getent; /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group.
Automate system administration tasks by scheduling jobs
Weight 4. crontab and /etc/cron.*, at, cron.allow and cron.deny, and systemd timers.
Localisation and internationalisation
Weight 3. Locales (LANG, LC_ALL), time zones with timedatectl and /etc/localtime, UTF-8 and iconv.

domains.name: Essential System Services
obj: Maintain system time
Weight 3. date, hwclock and timedatectl; NTP with chrony or ntpd.
System logging
Weight 4. rsyslog facilities and priorities, logger, logrotate, and querying the journal with journalctl.
Mail Transfer Agent (MTA) basics
Weight 3. Aliases and forwarding with ~/.forward and newaliases; mail and mailq; Postfix, Sendmail and Exim.
Manage printers and printing
Weight 2. CUPS, lpr, lpq and lprm.

domains.name: Networking Fundamentals
obj: Fundamentals of internet protocols
Weight 4. Subnetting and CIDR, private ranges, TCP vs UDP vs ICMP, common ports, IPv4 vs IPv6.
Persistent network configuration
Weight 4. NetworkManager and nmcli, hostnamectl, /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf and /etc/nsswitch.conf.
Basic network troubleshooting
Weight 4. ip, ss, ping, traceroute, tracepath and netcat; the older ifconfig, netstat and route.
Configure client side DNS
Weight 2. host, dig and getent; resolution order; systemd-resolved.

domains.name: Security
obj: Perform security administration tasks
Weight 3. Find SUID and SGID files, password aging, open ports (ss, lsof, nmap), ulimit, who is logged in, and sudo.
Setup host security
Weight 3. Shadow passwords, turning off unused services, /etc/nologin, TCP wrappers.
Securing data with encryption
Weight 4. OpenSSH client and keys (ssh-keygen, ssh-agent), host keys, SSH tunnels, and GnuPG to encrypt, sign and verify.

pbqs.title: Same task, two package families
pbqs.scenario: Your shop runs Ubuntu and Rocky Linux servers. For each task, pick the command for each family.

rows.req: Install nmap from the configured repositories.
rows.why: apt-get install nmap on Debian; dnf install nmap on Rocky (yum on older releases).

rows.req: Find which installed package owns /usr/bin/curl.
rows.why: dpkg -S /usr/bin/curl and rpm -qf /usr/bin/curl both map a file to its package.

rows.req: List every file the openssh-server package installed.
rows.why: dpkg -L openssh-server and rpm -ql openssh-server list a package's files.

rows.req: Install a vendor's agent from a downloaded package file.
rows.why: dpkg -i agent.deb and rpm -i agent.rpm install a local file. (dnf install ./agent.rpm also works and pulls dependencies.)

rows.req: Refresh the list of available packages before patching.
rows.why: apt-get update downloads fresh package lists; dnf check-update refreshes metadata and shows pending updates.

pbqs.title: Triage six server problems
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from a different server ticket. Pick what it shows. Each answer is used once; two are distractors.

items.log:
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda3        20G   20G     0 100% /var
items.why: /var is at 100%. Logs and databases there will start failing. Find the space with du and clean or grow it.

items.log: kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 4812 (java) total-vm:8123456kB, anon-rss:6020112kB
items.why: The kernel's OOM killer ended the biggest process to free memory. Check free -m and the app's memory settings.
MySQL accepts connections only from the same host. Remote app servers will be refused until it listens on a network address.

items.log: -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 1183448 Nov  9 03:12 /tmp/.cache/bash
items.why: A SUID-root copy of bash hidden in /tmp gives anyone a root shell. Classic attacker persistence: escalate it as an incident.

items.log: 10.20.0.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.20.0.15
items.why: Only the local subnet route exists. With no default route, the host can't reach anything off 10.20.0.0/24.

items.log: EXT4-fs error (device sdb1): ext4_lookup:1601: inode #131074: comm ls: deleted inode referenced: 131590
items.why: The kernel found file system corruption. Unmount the file system and run fsck (e2fsck) on it.

keep.text: LPIC-1 stays active for 5 years. Renew it by passing the current 101 and 102 again, by earning LPIC-2 (which renews LPIC-1 to the same date), or with an LPI membership plus 20 professional development units (PDUs) a year.
keep.after: Your LPIC-1 must still be active when you earn LPIC-2.

keep.text: LPIC-1 isn't on the DoD 8140 qualification matrix, so on its own it won't qualify you for a coded billet.
keep.after: Pair it with a cert that is on the matrix, such as Security+. Some positions also want proof you can run the operating system you'll manage, and LPIC-1 shows that for Linux.

keep.text: Most cloud servers run Linux. LPIC-1 plus an AWS or Azure cert is a strong pair for cloud admin and cloud security jobs.
keep.after: Use CG COOL for both vouchers.

v5.label: V5
v5.note: The only version on sale. CompTIA hasn't announced a retirement date or a new version yet. It says exams usually retire about three years after launch, so check the exam page before you buy a voucher.
v5.onote: Official CompTIA objectives (PK0-005), in plain words. Domain weights are from CompTIA's exam page.

domains.name: Project Management Concepts
obj: Project characteristics, methodologies and frameworks
Projects are temporary and unique, with a start and finish; programs and portfolios; waterfall, Scrum, Kanban, XP, SAFe, PRINCE2, DevOps, DevSecOps and the SDLC.
Agile vs waterfall
Choosing by tolerance for change, how clear the requirements are, budget and schedule; team makeup and roles; how communication differs.
Change control
Log and review change requests, assess the impact, take them to the decision maker or change control board, update the plan, then validate and communicate. Product vs project change; scope creep.
Risk management
Known and unknown risks; qualitative vs quantitative analysis; responses to threats (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) and opportunities (exploit, enhance, share, accept); risk owners.
Issue management
Issue logs, owners and escalation paths; root cause analysis, contingency plans and workarounds; documenting the outcome.
Schedule development and management
Milestones, activities and sprint goals; dependencies like finish-to-start; estimates, story points and buffers; critical path; revise the baseline vs rebaseline.
Quality and performance management
Retrospectives and lessons learned; SLAs, KPIs and OKRs; cost and schedule variance; audits; unit, smoke, regression, stress and user acceptance testing.
Communication management
Synchronous vs asynchronous, formal vs informal, internal vs external; time zones and language; keeping records; revising the communication plan.
Meeting management
Workshops, stand-ups, demos, status and steering meetings; agendas, timeboxing, facilitator and scribe; minutes and action items.
Team and resource management
Functional, matrix and projectized organizations; resource gaps; forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning; sponsor, product owner, Scrum master, SMEs.
Procurement and vendor selection
Build, buy, lease or subscribe; RFI, RFQ, RFP and RFB; best value vs lowest cost; fixed price, time and materials, cost plus; MSA, SOW, PO and NDA.

domains.name: Project Life Cycle Phases
obj: Discovery and concept artifacts
Business case and ROI, current vs future state, prequalified vendors and existing contracts, SOWs, CapEx vs OpEx.
Initiation
Project charter with objectives, success criteria and preliminary scope; stakeholders; a RACI matrix; access requirements; the kickoff meeting.
Planning
Assign resources; communication plan, scope statement, WBS or backlog, schedule, budget, quality plan, risk assessment, transition and release plans; baselines.
Execution
Work the plan; organizational change (training, adoption); manage vendors; track progress, budget and timeline; resolve conflict; phase gate reviews.
Closing
Validate deliverables, close contracts, remove access, release resources, write the closeout report, archive documents, reconcile the budget, get sign-off.

domains.name: Tools and Documentation
obj: Project tools
Gantt, burndown, PERT and network diagrams, milestone charts; issue, defect and change logs; risk register; status reports, dashboards, task boards and a requirements traceability matrix.
Productivity tools
Communication, collaboration, meeting, office, scheduling and ticketing tools, in the cloud or on premises.
Quality and performance charts
Histograms, Pareto, run, control and scatter charts, fishbone diagrams, burnup and burndown, velocity charts and decision trees.

domains.name: Basics of IT and Governance
obj: ESG factors
A project's effect on the environment, regulations and standards, company values and brand.
Information security
Physical (devices, media, facility access), operational (screening, clearances), digital (permissions, remote access, MFA) and data security (classification, need to know).
Compliance and privacy
PII and PHI, legal and regulatory requirements, privacy laws by country and state, industry rules.
IT concepts
Infrastructure (compute, multitier, networking, storage), IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, and enterprise software like ERP, CRM and databases.
Operational change control
Maintenance windows, user notifications, rollback plans and validation checks; software change approval and testing; CI/CD; production vs staging.

pbqs.title: Name the phase and the document
pbqs.scenario: You're running a network refresh for your unit. For each moment, pick the phase you're in and the document you'd use.

rows.req: Leadership wants to know why the refresh is worth funding: costs, ROI, and today vs after.
rows.why: The business case justifies the project during discovery, before it's approved.

rows.req: The commanding officer formally approves the project and names you project manager.
rows.why: The charter authorizes the project and the PM. It's the key initiation document.

rows.req: Decide who does, who owns, who's asked and who's told for each task.
rows.why: The RACI is built in initiation, alongside identifying stakeholders.

rows.req: Break the scope into small work packages the team can estimate.
rows.why: The work breakdown structure is a planning document.

rows.req: The switches arrive damaged. You record it, assign an owner and track it to resolution.
rows.why: A problem happening now is an issue, tracked in the issue log during execution.

rows.req: Record the results, the lessons learned and the sign-off.
rows.why: The closeout report wraps up the project.

pbqs.title: Pick the risk response
pbqs.scenario: Each line is a decision you made on a project. Pick the risk response. Each answer is used once; one is a distractor.

items.text: Your only firewall expert might transfer mid-project. You pair a second tech with them now so the knowledge isn't lost.
items.why: Mitigate: you can't stop the transfer, but you lower its impact.

items.text: Migrating an unsupported old system could break the cutover, so you drop it from scope.
items.why: Avoid: changing the scope removes the risk entirely.

items.text: The contract makes the vendor pay for any delay their late hardware causes.
items.why: Transfer: the financial impact shifts to the vendor through the contract.

items.text: There's a small chance the training room projector fails. You decide to live with it.
items.why: Accept: the impact is low, so you take no action now.

items.text: A sister unit is buying the same licenses. You combine the orders so both units get the volume discount.
items.why: Share: you team up with another party to capture an opportunity.

items.text: Finishing early would let your unit join a pilot program. You add a second shift to raise the odds.
items.why: Enhance: you raise the chance of the good outcome without guaranteeing it.

pbqs.title: Choose the chart
pbqs.scenario: Each request came from your sponsor. Pick the chart or tool that answers it. Each answer is used once; two are distractors.

items.text: Show every task on a timeline with its dates and dependencies.
items.why: A Gantt chart shows tasks as bars over time, with dependencies.

items.text: Show how much sprint work is left each day compared with the ideal pace.
items.why: A burndown chart tracks remaining work against an ideal line.

items.text: Find the few causes behind most of the outage tickets.
items.why: A Pareto chart sorts causes by count with a cumulative line.

items.text: Brainstorm every possible cause of slow logins, grouped by people, process and technology.
items.why: A fishbone (cause and effect) diagram groups possible causes of one problem.

items.text: Check whether more users online means longer page load times.
items.why: A scatter diagram shows whether two variables move together.

items.text: Compare the expected value of buying vs leasing, with the chances of each outcome.
items.why: A decision tree weighs options by probability and value.

Lower the chance or the impact

Do nothing now; keep a contingency ready
Raise the chance or the benefit
Team up with someone who can help capture it

tips: Follow the process
When a stakeholder asks for a change, the answer is almost never “just do it.” It goes through change control.
Know the phase
Many questions are really asking which phase you're in. Name the phase first, then pick the action.
Read the qualifier
FIRST, BEST and NEXT change the answer. Several options can be true; only one fits the qualifier.
Flag the PBQs
Performance-based questions can eat time. Flag them, finish the multiple choice, then come back.

c02.label: C02
c02.note: The only version on sale. AWS hasn't announced a CLF-C03. AWS posts exam guide changes about a month before they reach the exam, so check the exam page before you book.
c02.onote: Official AWS task statements (CLF-C02 exam guide), in plain words. Weights are AWS's share of scored content.

domains.name: Cloud Concepts
obj: Benefits of the AWS Cloud
Pay only for what you use, AWS's lower prices from huge scale, speed and agility, going global in minutes, high availability and elasticity, and no more guessing how much hardware to buy.
Design principles
The six pillars of the Well-Architected Framework: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability.
Migration benefits and strategies

The Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) and its perspectives; migration strategies such as rehost (lift and shift), replatform, refactor, repurchase, retain and retire; tools like the Snow Family and Database Migration Service.
Cloud economics

Fixed vs variable cost; on-premises costs you stop paying, like power, cooling and hardware refresh; licensing (bring your own vs included); right-sizing; the value of managed services and automation.

domains.name: Security and Compliance
obj: The shared responsibility model

AWS secures the cloud itself: buildings, hardware, the network and the services' software. You secure what you put in it: your data, IAM, security groups and, on EC2, the operating system. The split shifts by service (EC2 vs RDS vs Lambda).
Security, governance and compliance concepts
Where AWS's compliance reports live (AWS Artifact); encryption at rest and in transit; audit and governance tools like CloudTrail, Config, CloudWatch and Audit Manager.
Access management

IAM users, groups, roles and policies; least privilege; lock down the root user with MFA and don't use it day to day; IAM Identity Center for single sign-on; access keys vs passwords; Secrets Manager.
Security components and resources
Security groups, network ACLs, AWS WAF, Shield, GuardDuty, Inspector, Security Hub and Detective; Trusted Advisor checks; AWS Marketplace security tools; security blogs and the Knowledge Center.

domains.name: Cloud Technology and Services
obj: Deploying and operating
Console, CLI, SDKs and APIs; infrastructure as code with CloudFormation; cloud, hybrid and on-premises deployment models; connecting with Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect.
Global infrastructure
Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations; why two or more AZs give high availability; picking a Region for law, latency, cost and the services you need.
Compute services
EC2 and its instance families, Auto Scaling and Elastic Load Balancing; containers with ECS, EKS and Fargate; serverless with Lambda; Elastic Beanstalk.
Database services
RDS and Aurora (relational), DynamoDB (NoSQL key-value), ElastiCache (in-memory), Neptune (graph); managed databases vs installing your own on EC2; the Database Migration Service.
Network services
VPC, public and private subnets, route tables, internet and NAT gateways; security groups vs network ACLs; Route 53 (DNS); CloudFront and Global Accelerator; VPN and Direct Connect.
Storage services
S3 and its storage classes and lifecycle rules; EBS volumes for EC2; EFS shared file storage; FSx; Storage Gateway for hybrid; AWS Backup.
AI/ML and analytics services
What SageMaker AI, Bedrock, Rekognition, Comprehend, Lex, Polly and Textract do; analytics with Athena, Kinesis, Glue, Redshift, EMR and QuickSight.
Other service categories
Messaging (SQS, SNS, EventBridge), developer tools (CodeBuild, CodePipeline), end-user computing (WorkSpaces), web and mobile front ends (Amplify), IoT Core and Amazon Connect.

domains.name: Billing, Pricing, and Support
obj: Pricing models
On-Demand, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, Spot Instances, Dedicated Hosts and Dedicated Instances; data coming in is free, data going out costs; storage tiers.
Billing, budget and cost tools
Billing console, AWS Budgets, Cost Explorer, the Cost and Usage Report and the Pricing Calculator; consolidated billing in AWS Organizations; cost allocation tags.
Technical resources and Support
AWS Support plans and what each adds; technical account managers; Trusted Advisor; AWS Health Dashboard; re:Post, the Knowledge Center and Prescriptive Guidance; AWS Partners and Marketplace.

pbqs.title: Who's responsible?
pbqs.scenario: Your unit runs workloads on EC2, RDS and S3. For each task, pick who is responsible under the shared responsibility model.

rows.req: Patch the operating system on an EC2 instance
rows.why: On EC2 you control the OS, so patching it is yours.

rows.req: Patch the database engine on Amazon RDS
rows.why: RDS is managed. AWS patches the engine and the OS under it.

rows.req: Replace a failed hard drive in an AWS data center
rows.why: Hardware is always AWS's job.

rows.req: Turn on encryption for sensitive data in an S3 bucket
rows.why: AWS gives you the tools. Deciding to use them, and how, is yours.

rows.req: Set the inbound rules on a security group
rows.why: You configure security groups. If you can change it, you own it.

rows.req: Train people on security and patch management
rows.why: These are shared controls: AWS trains its staff and patches its side; you train yours and patch your side.

pbqs.title: Pick the service
pbqs.scenario: Each request came from your division chief. Pick the AWS service that does it. Each answer is used once; four are distractors.

items.text: Show who deleted the training bucket, and when.
items.why: CloudTrail records API calls: who, what, when and from where.

items.text: Alarm when a server's CPU stays above 90% for 10 minutes.
items.why: CloudWatch collects metrics and runs alarms.

items.text: Serve our training videos quickly to sailors around the world.
items.why: CloudFront caches content at edge locations close to users.

items.text: Point training.example.com at our app and fail over to a backup site.
items.why: Route 53 is AWS's DNS, with health checks and failover routing.

items.text: Keep 50 TB of log archives we rarely read, as cheaply as possible.
items.why: S3, with a Glacier storage class, is built for cheap long-term storage.

items.text: Run a PostgreSQL database with automatic backups, without patching it ourselves.
items.why: RDS is the managed relational database service.

pbqs.title: Pick the pricing model
pbqs.scenario: Five workloads are coming to AWS. Pick the cheapest EC2 pricing model that still fits each one.

rows.req: A web server that will run 24/7 for the next three years
rows.why: A 1 or 3 year commitment gives the biggest discount on steady, always-on use.

rows.req: A two-week test of a new app; nobody knows the load
rows.why: Short and unpredictable: pay as you go with no commitment.

rows.req: Rendering jobs that can be interrupted and picked up later
rows.why: Interruptible work is what Spot is for.

rows.req: Software licensed per physical CPU socket
rows.why: A Dedicated Host gives you a whole physical server so you can use per-socket licenses.

rows.req: Extra capacity for a one-week exercise that must not be interrupted
rows.why: Too short for a commitment, and it can't risk Spot interruptions.

extras.title: Global infrastructure
rows: A separate geographic area with 3+ AZs. Pick it for law, latency, cost and services
One or more data centers with their own power and network. Spread apps across 2+
CloudFront and Route 53 serve users from here, close to them
AWS compute placed close to a big city for low latency
AWS racks installed in your own data center

extras.title: Pricing models
rows: No commitment. Short, spiky or unknown workloads
Commit to an hourly spend; flexible across instance types
Commit to an instance type; steady workloads
Up to 90% off, but AWS can take it back with a 2-minute warning
Per-socket licenses or rules that need your own hardware

extras.title: Lock down a new account
rows: Turn on MFA for the root user. Don't create root access keys.
Create admin access through IAM Identity Center (or an IAM role), and stop using root.
Create a CloudTrail trail so API history is kept longer than the 90-day default.
Set an AWS Budgets alert before you launch anything.
Turn on GuardDuty and look at Trusted Advisor's security checks.

extras.title: Support plans
rows: Docs, re:Post, the Health Dashboard and core Trusted Advisor checks
24/7 cases; AWS aims to answer critical issues within 30 minutes
Adds a technical account manager; 15 minutes for critical issues
A designated AWS team; 5 minutes for critical issues
Developer, Business and Enterprise On-Ramp. The CLF-C02 guide still uses these names

tips: Match the keyword
“Managed,” “serverless” and “least effort” point to the AWS service that runs it for you, not EC2.
Who owns it?
For shared responsibility questions, ask: can I touch it? If you can configure it, it's yours.
Choose all that apply
Multiple response questions tell you how many to pick. No partial credit, so check you picked exactly that many.
Don't overthink
This is a breadth exam. If an answer needs deep design trade-offs, it's probably a distractor.

c03.note: The only version on sale. AWS hasn't announced an SAA-C04. AWS refreshed the exam guide's service lists in 2026 (latest Oct 29, 2026), and changes reach the exam about a month after they're posted, so study from the current guide.
c03.onote: Official AWS task statements (SAA-C03 exam guide), in plain words. Weights are AWS's share of scored content.

domains.name: Design Secure Architectures
obj: Secure access to AWS resources

IAM users, groups, roles and policies; least privilege; MFA and root protection; IAM Identity Center and federation; cross-account roles; AWS Organizations with service control policies (SCPs); temporary credentials from STS.
Secure workloads and applications

VPC design with public and private subnets; security groups and network ACLs; WAF, Shield and GuardDuty; Cognito for app sign-in; Secrets Manager; VPN and Direct Connect; VPC endpoints to keep traffic off the internet.
Data security controls
Encryption at rest and in transit with KMS and ACM; key rotation; S3 bucket policies, Block Public Access and Object Lock; backup and retention; finding sensitive data with Macie.

domains.name: Design Resilient Architectures
obj: Scalable and loosely coupled architectures
Decouple tiers with SQS, SNS and EventBridge; API Gateway; serverless with Lambda and Fargate; containers; Auto Scaling; caching; stateless designs; Step Functions workflows.
Highly available and fault-tolerant architectures

Multi-AZ and multi-Region designs; load balancers; Route 53 health checks and failover; RDS Multi-AZ and read replicas; disaster recovery strategies chosen by RTO and RPO; no single points of failure.

domains.name: Design High-Performing Architectures
obj: High-performing storage
S3, EBS volume types, EFS and FSx; picking by access pattern, throughput and IOPS; S3 Transfer Acceleration and multipart upload.
High-performing and elastic compute
EC2 instance families and sizes, Auto Scaling, Lambda, containers on ECS and EKS, Fargate; decoupling so each tier scales on its own.
High-performing databases
RDS vs Aurora vs DynamoDB; read replicas; RDS Proxy; caching with ElastiCache and DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX); picking the engine and capacity.
High-performing networks
CloudFront and Global Accelerator; VPC subnets and routing; Transit Gateway, VPC peering and PrivateLink; load balancer types; Direct Connect and VPN.
Data ingestion and transformation
Streaming with Kinesis; ETL with Glue; querying S3 with Athena; data lakes with Lake Formation; moving data with DataSync and the Snow Family; dashboards with QuickSight.

domains.name: Design Cost-Optimized Architectures
obj: Cost-optimized storage
S3 storage classes, lifecycle rules and Intelligent-Tiering; right-sized EBS volumes; backup retention; tracking with Cost Explorer and Budgets.
Cost-optimized compute
On-Demand vs Savings Plans vs Reserved vs Spot; right-sizing; Graviton instances; Auto Scaling to match demand; Lambda for spiky loads.
Cost-optimized databases
Right-size DB instances; Aurora Serverless and DynamoDB on-demand for unpredictable loads; reserved DB capacity; snapshot and backup retention costs.
Cost-optimized networks
Data transfer between AZs, Regions and the internet; NAT gateway costs vs free gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB; CloudFront to cut origin traffic; Direct Connect vs VPN.

pbqs.title: Fix the architecture
pbqs.scenario: A design review found six problems in your unit's AWS app. Pick the change that fixes each one. Each fix is used once; two are distractors.

rows.req: The web tier is one EC2 instance. When it fails, the site is down.
rows.why: A load balancer across AZs plus Auto Scaling replaces failed instances and spreads load.

rows.req: The database is one RDS instance in one AZ.
rows.why: Multi-AZ adds a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover.

rows.req: Orders are lost when the processing tier falls behind.
rows.why: A queue holds orders until a worker is free.

rows.req: Pictures load slowly for users in Europe and Asia.
rows.why: CloudFront caches content at edge locations near users.

rows.req: Private instances reach S3 through an expensive NAT gateway.
rows.why: A gateway endpoint sends S3 traffic privately at no extra charge.

rows.req: Years of old logs sit in S3 Standard.
rows.why: A lifecycle rule moves old data to cheaper classes and deletes it on schedule.

pbqs.title: Pick the recovery strategy
pbqs.scenario: Five systems need a recovery plan. Pick the cheapest strategy that still meets each requirement. One choice is a distractor.

items.text: Can be down for a day. Losing a day of changes is fine. Cheapest possible.
items.why: Backups copied to another Region are the cheapest, and hours of downtime are acceptable.

items.text: The database must replicate all the time, but app servers can stay off until needed. Back within about an hour.
items.why: Pilot light keeps only the core data running and starts the rest during recovery.

items.text: Must be back within minutes. A smaller full copy may run all the time.
items.why: Warm standby runs a scaled-down working copy ready to scale up.

items.text: No downtime allowed, even if a whole Region fails. Both Regions serve users.
items.why: Only active/active in two Regions gives near-zero downtime for a Region failure.

items.text: Must survive one data center failing. A Region-wide outage is an accepted risk.
items.why: Spreading across AZs in one Region handles a data center failure without paying for a second Region.

pbqs.title: Pick the database
pbqs.scenario: Six teams are choosing databases. Pick the best fit for each. Each choice is used once; one is a distractor.

rows.req: A relational order system with steady load that needs automatic failover
rows.why: RDS with Multi-AZ is the standard choice for steady relational workloads that must fail over.

rows.req: A relational app used a few hours a week with unpredictable spikes
rows.why: Aurora Serverless scales capacity with demand, so you don't pay for idle hours.

rows.req: A shopping cart for millions of users with millisecond reads at any scale
rows.why: DynamoDB is serverless key-value storage built for that scale.

rows.req: A session store that needs microsecond reads
rows.why: ElastiCache keeps data in memory for the fastest reads.

rows.req: Analysts run SQL over years of sales data
rows.why: Redshift is the data warehouse for analytics on large data sets.

rows.req: Find “friends of friends” and other relationship queries
rows.why: Neptune is a graph database built for relationships.
